Abstract:
Low performance is considered one of the main drawbacks of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) technology. In the present work, the effect of the AlSi10Mg powder layer thickness on the laser melting process was investigated to improve the LPBF building rate. A high-fidelity simulation of the melt pool formation was performed for different thicknesses of the powder bed using the Kintech Simulation Software for Additive Manufacturing (KiSSAM, version cd8e01d) developed by the authors. The powder bed after the recoating operation was obtained by the discrete element method. The laser energy deposition on the powder particles and the substrate was simulated by ray tracing. For the validation of the model, an experimental analysis of single tracks was performed on two types of substrates. The first substrate was manufactured directly with LPBF technology, while the second was cast. The simulation was carried out for various combinations of process parameters, predominantly with a high energy input, which provided a sufficient remelting depth. The calculations revealed the unstable keyhole mode appearance associated with the low absorptivity of the aluminum alloy at a scanning speed of 300 mm/s for all levels of the laser power (325–375 W). The results allowed formulating the criteria for the lack of fusion emerging during LPBF with an increased layer thickness. This work is expected to provide a scientific basis for the analysis of the maximum layer thickness via simulation to increase the performance of the technology.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Powder bed fusion (PBF) is a widely adopted additive manufacturing (AM) process category that enables high-resolution fabrication across metals, polymers, ceramics, and composites. However, its inherent process complexity demands robust modeling to ensure quality, reliability, and scalability. This review provides a critical synthesis of advances in physics-based simulations, machine learning, and digital twin frameworks for PBF. We analyze progress across scales—from micro-scale melt pool dynamics and mesoscale track stability to part-scale residual stress predictions—while highlighting the growing role of hybrid physics–data-driven approaches in capturing process–structure–property (PSP) relationships. Special emphasis is given to the integration of real-time sensing, multi-scale modeling, and AI-enhanced optimization, which together form the foundation of emerging PBF digital twins. Key challenges—including computational cost, data scarcity, and model interoperability—are critically examined, alongside opportunities for scalable, interpretable, and industry-ready digital twin platforms. By outlining both the current state-of-the-art and future research priorities, this review positions digital twins as a transformative paradigm for advancing PBF toward reliable, high-quality, and industrially scalable manufacturing.</jats:p>

AG", issue = "23", issn = "1996-1944" } Abstract: Despite the significant advances made involving the additive manufacturing (AM) of metals, including those related to both materials and processes, challenges remain in regard to the rapid qualification and insertion of such materials into applications. In general, understanding the process–microstructure–property interrelationships is essential. To successfully understand these interrelationships on a process-by-process basis and exploit such knowledge in practice, leveraging monitoring, modeling, and statistical analysis is necessary. Monitoring allows for the identification and measurement of parameters and features associated with important physical processes that may vary spatially and temporally during the AM processes that will influence part properties, including spatial variations within a single part and part-to-part variability, and, ultimately, quality. Modeling allows for the prediction of physical processes, material states, and properties of future builds by creating material state abstractions that can then be tested or evolved virtually. Statistical analysis permits the data from monitoring to inform modeling, and vice versa, under the added consideration that physical measurements and mathematical abstractions contain uncertainties. Throughout this review, the feedstock, energy source, melt pool, defects, compositional distribution, microstructure, texture, residual stresses, and mechanical properties are examined from the points of view of monitoring, modeling, and statistical analysis. As with most active research subjects, there remain both possibilities and limitations, and these will be considered and discussed as appropriate. Over the past decades, the field has increasingly embraced the application of artificial intelligence methodologies, thus recognising their suitability in forecasting non-linear relationships intrinsic to materials. This review offers a critical evaluation AI methodologies incorporated in computational mechanics for geotechnical engineering. The analysis categorises four pivotal areas: physical properties, mechanical properties, constitutive models, and other characteristics relevant to geotechnical materials. Among the various methodologies analysed, ANNs stand out as the most commonly used strategy, while other methods such as SVMs, LSTMs, and CNNs also see a significant level of application. The most widely used AI algorithms are Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Random Forest (RF), and Support Vector Machines (SVM), representing 35%, 19%, and 17% respectively. The most extensive AI application is in the domain of mechanical properties, accounting for 59%, followed by other applications at 16%. The efficacy of AI applications is intrinsically linked to the type of datasets employed, the selected model input. This study also outlines future research directions emphasising the need to integrate physically guided and adaptive learning mechanisms to enhance the reliability and adaptability in addressing multi-scale and multi-physics coupled mechanics problems in geotechnics. The engineering demand for lightweighting in police protective equipment is fundamentally a constrained multi-objective optimization problem, requiring balanced trade-offs among protective performance, functional performance, durability, and manufacturing constraints. Conventional trial-and-error design approaches for high-performance fiber-reinforced composites—such as ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMWPE), aramid, and carbon fiber systems—are costly and inefficient due to complex multi-parameter interactions governing ballistic limit velocity (V₅₀) and back-face signature (BFS). This study presents a systematic machine learning (ML)-driven framework for lightweight material design tailored to law enforcement protective gear. A unified data preparation and feature engineering methodology was established by synthesizing information across scientific literature, institutional databases, experimental measurements, and numerical simulations, constructing a multi-dimensional dataset encompassing 3,247 physical samples across 8 material categories described by 34 input features. A comparative evaluation of predictive algorithms—including XGBoost, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbors, and Physics-Informed Neural Networks—demonstrated that XGBoost achieved the highest generalization accuracy (R² = 0.942) for ballistic performance prediction. SHAP (Shapley Additive exPlanations) analysis identified fiber volume fraction, layup orientation, and matrix selection as the dominant features governing protective performance. A multi-objective optimization framework integrating ML surrogate models with the NSGA-II evolutionary algorithm and active learning strategies was implemented to minimize mass under strict protective constraints, reducing required experimental iterations by 60% compared to conventional grid search methods. Physical validation across 15 material formulations and 3 equipment prototypes confirmed that the ML-optimized designs achieved weight reductions of 20–33% compared to baseline commercial systems without compromising structural integrity: soft body armor achieved a 25% mass reduction alongside a 2.9% increase in V₅₀ and a 14% decrease in BFS depth; ballistic helmets attained a 20.7% mass reduction at equivalent protection levels; riot shields realized a 33.3% weight reduction with a 20% improvement in impact resistance. These findings establish ML-driven methodologies as a transformative approach for accelerated, cost-effective, and high-performance lightweight material design in protective equipment applications.

## pqac-00000015

From text 'haapa2023validationofpowder pages 5-7'.

E. Haapa, A. Gopaluni, H. Piili, A. Ganvir, A. Salminen, and J. Ottelin. Validation of powder layering simulation via packing density measurement for laser-based powder bed fusion. IOP Conference Series: Materials Science and Engineering, Dec 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899x/1296/1/012020, doi:10.1088/1757-899x/1296/1/012020. This article has 1 citations.

Haapa et al. validate a DEM powder-layering simulation against experimentally measured powder-bed density (PD) for Alloy 718 on an EOS M 290 using a 40 µm layer height. The experiment uses an open-cup sample positioned centrally near the dispenser. Powder mass is bounded by minimum, measured, and maximum estimates obtained from successive weighing and cleaning steps; sample volume is calculated from measured dimensions, and PD is computed from powder volume divided by sample volume. Across five samples, the experimental mean PD was 52.2% for PDmin (standard deviation 0.29%), 52.4% for PDmeasured (0.20%), and 52.4% for PDmax (0.22%). The nominal-CAD-volume estimate was higher and more variable: 53.2% mean with 0.56% standard deviation. The DEM model contains approximately 260,000 particles recoated in four 40 µm layers, uses the real recoater geometry and speed, and incorporates supplier PSD and density data plus calibrated/approximated contact parameters. Simulation density is evaluated using embedded-volume, powder-bed-extents, and intermediate definitions (PDmax-sim, PDmin-sim, and PDmeasured-sim), with both full-bed and central stable-area sampling. The excerpt does not provide the simulated PD numerical results or an explicit experiment–simulation agreement/error, so quantitative validation agreement cannot be calculated from these pages alone.

## pqac-00000016

From text 'lee2020effectofparticle pages 9-11'.

Yousub Lee, A. Kate Gurnon, David Bodner, and Srdjan Simunovic. Effect of particle spreading dynamics on powder bed quality in metal additive manufacturing. Integrating Materials and Manufacturing Innovation, 9:410-422, Nov 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40192-020-00193-1, doi:10.1007/s40192-020-00193-1. This article has 70 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Lee et al. (2020) provide DEM validation against several experimental observables relevant to powder-bed quality. The strongest numerical agreement is for powder-bed height: the predicted height matches the measured value within a 1% error range. Dynamic angle of repose (AOR) is also compared over time; although the experiment shows an initial abrupt increase attributed potentially to atmospheric moisture and cohesive-bond effects, the model reproduces the subsequent variation reasonably well. Experimental and simulated powder-pile images are compared at multiple spreading positions. Both show progressive pile-volume reduction as the rake moves the powder, and both reproduce the plateau region at the pile top and its disappearance during spreading. For particle-size distribution (PSD), the initial simulated distribution corresponds to measurements, while measured and predicted PSDs are compared before and during deposition. The model predicts coarsening in the pile ahead of the rake during spreading and reports a finer PSD shift with increasing rake velocity in the recoating layer. The excerpt does not provide a direct numerical validation of captured mass or measured topography, and packing-density results appear primarily predictive rather than experimentally quantified. It reports approximately a 5% simulated density decrease when rake velocity is increased fivefold, alongside qualitative experimental surface-uniformity comparisons.

## pqac-00000017

From text 'haapa2023validationofpowder pages 9-11'.

E. Haapa, A. Gopaluni, H. Piili, A. Ganvir, A. Salminen, and J. Ottelin. Validation of powder layering simulation via packing density measurement for laser-based powder bed fusion. IOP Conference Series: Materials Science and Engineering, Dec 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899x/1296/1/012020, doi:10.1088/1757-899x/1296/1/012020. This article has 1 citations.

For Haapa et al.’s powder-layering validation, the study-specific experimental evidence is an open-cup powder-density measurement using Alloy 718 powder, compared with a simulated powder bed. Across five samples, the measured packing density (PD) had a mean of 52.4% and a standard deviation of 0.20%. The authors state that this result was a good match to the simulated powder bed, even though the experimental sample was orders of magnitude larger. They conclude that uncertainty associated with the simulation was more influential than uncertainty from the validation measurement, supporting the method as sufficiently accurate and reliable for validating powder-bed simulation models. The excerpt does not provide the simulated PD value, an absolute or percentage deviation between measured and simulated density, or evidence involving captured mass, imaging, topography, or segregation. It also contains no study-specific results for Shahed binder jetting, Zhang roller, Brika, or Lee 2020; those comparisons would require the corresponding excerpts or full papers. The cited literature includes several powder-spreading and powder-bed-density studies, but the provided pages only establish Haapa’s numerical experimental result and qualitative agreement with simulation.

## pqac-00000018

From text 'shahed2025powderspreadingbehavior pages 10-11'.

Kazi Safowan Shahed, Willem Groeneveld-Meijer, Matthew Lear, Jeremy Schreiber, and Guha Manogharan. Powder spreading behavior of bimodal ceramics in the binder jetting process. Materials Science in Additive Manufacturing, 4:025110016, May 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.36922/msam025110016, doi:10.36922/msam025110016. This article has 8 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

For Shahed et al. (2025), the excerpt provides study-specific DEM–experiment agreement primarily for segregation and directional powder-bed density trends. Discrete element simulations and experiments both showed that, in the 5 µm/20 µm bimodal ceramic powder, fine particles preferentially settled at the beginning of spreading while coarse particles migrated toward the trailing edge. Both approaches also indicated a decreasing packing-density trend along the spreading direction, with denser fine-particle-dominated regions and looser coarse-particle-dominated regions. The excerpt reports quantitative experimental density values: the overall powder-bed packing density was approximately 0.6651, while measurements perpendicular to spreading were nearly uniform at Y1 = 0.6516, Y2 = 0.6521, and Y3 = 0.6512, with an average of 0.6517. It also states that spatial packing-density fluctuations were reflected in green-part density variations. However, the provided pages do not give a numerical error, correlation coefficient, or point-by-point DEM-versus-experiment comparison, nor do they report captured mass, imaging metrics, or topography-based validation. Thus, this excerpt supports qualitative validation of segregation and density-gradient patterns, with measured density values available as experimental benchmarks but no quantified DEM agreement.

The excerpt defines DEM validation as replicating the model or its core components experimentally, measuring both simulation and experiment, and comparing the results within a specified error margin. It recommends quantitative validation, while noting that qualitative validation is often used to reduce computational and experimental effort. The validation table identifies visual comparison of powder beds for Han et al. (2019) as partial validation of spread and AOR comparison for Meier et al. (2019) as successful flow validation. It also lists Tian et al. (2020) as visually comparing melt tracks, but explicitly says recoating was not the focus and was therefore not validated. Dai et al. (2019, 2021) and Phua et al. (2021) are listed as not validated. The supplied pages do not contain study-specific numerical agreement values for experimental powder-bed density, captured mass, imaging, topography, or segregation, nor do they provide results for Shahed binder jetting, Brika, or Lee (2020). Zhang et al. (2020) appears in the calibration discussion as studying roller parameters and packing density, but no numerical validation agreement is reported in this excerpt.

This excerpt provides one powder-spreading simulation example: a conventional, particle-resolved DEM model of a vertical blade spreading an idealized heap of spherical, mono-sized, non-cohesive Ti6AlV4 particles across a horizontal substrate through a thin gap. The modeled physics include particle motion, shear-induced dilation when motion begins, dilation and rearrangement as particles pass through the gap, and particle inertia in the deposited layer. It evaluates process effects from gap thickness, blade velocity, and the velocity profile in the shear layer. The principal measured or computed validation quantities are deposited-layer packing fraction and its reduction relative to the initial heap; the article also frames layer uniformity and packing density as important manufacturing properties. The reported trends are that larger gap thickness increases packing fraction, while higher blade velocity and higher mean normalized shear-layer velocity reduce it. The study is mechanistic and potentially adaptable to other materials, particle morphologies, and surface properties, but the excerpt does not report experimental validation. Its limits are substantial for comparison with coarse-grained DEM, CFD-DEM, binder-liquid, continuum granular, or MPM approaches: it represents dry, non-cohesive, monodisperse spherical particles, uses an idealized blade geometry, and contains no gas-flow, liquid-binder, continuum, or coarse-graining treatment. Therefore, it supports a dry DEM benchmark rather than examples of the other requested model classes.

DEM Simulation of the Powder

Vasileios Angelidakis, Michael Blank, Eric J. R. Parteli, Sudeshna Roy,
Daniel Schiochet Nasato, Hongyi Xiao, and Thorsten Pöschel





13.1  Introduction


The packing behavior of powders is signiﬁcantly inﬂuenced by various types of
inter-particle attractive forces, including adhesion and non-bonded van der Waals
forces [4, 7, 8, 19, 41, 43]. Alongside particle size and shape distributions, the inter-
particle interactions, particularly frictional and adhesive forces, play a crucial role
in determining the ﬂow behavior and consequently the packing density of the pow-
der layer. The impact of various types of attractive forces on the packing density of
powders with different materials and particle size distributions remains largely unex-
plored and requires further investigation. Accurately comprehending these effects
through experiments while considering speciﬁc particle size distributions and mate-
rial properties poses signiﬁcant challenges. To address these challenges, we employ
Discrete Element Method (DEM) simulations to characterize the packing behavior of
ﬁne powders. We can demonstrate quantitative agreement with experimental results
by incorporating the appropriate particle size distribution and using an adequate
model of attractive particle interactions. Furthermore, our ﬁndings indicate that both
adhesion, which is modeled using the Johnson-Kendall-Roberts (JKR) model [14],
and van der Waals interactions are crucial factors that must be taken into account in
DEM simulations.
   Characterization of the packing structure is essential to achieve simulation-driven
optimization of the layer quality. While local packing density is commonly employed
to characterize granular packings, relying solely on this parameter is inadequate for
identifying structural defects in disordered packings [33]. This is due to the fact that
numerous packing arrangements can exhibit the same local density. Conversely, local
structural anisotropy is a fundamental characteristic of non-crystalline packings and

late Systems, Cauerstraße 3, 91058 Erlangen, Germany
e-mail: thorsten.poeschel@fau.de

Manufacturing, Springer Tracts in Additive Manufacturing,

plays a signiﬁcant role in crucial mechanical properties within disordered packings,
such as jamming [34], plasticity [33], and shear band formation [10, 11, 42]. We use
local structural anisotropy as a measure to characterize the structures of the deposited
particles. This approach is threshold-free and provides a meaningful distribution that
accurately reﬂects the variations in the packing structure within a deposited powder
layer. It holds particular relevance in discerning the structural differences between
homogeneous packing observed in non-cohesive powders and the heterogeneous
packing tendencies prevalent in highly cohesive powders.
  The heat transfer within the powder bed is signiﬁcantly impacted by the quality
of the ﬁnal powder layer, including aspects such as the packing density and surface
proﬁle [44]. It is worth noting that many DEM simulations commonly disregard
the inﬂuence of temperature on inter-particle interaction forces. Nevertheless, it is
widely recognized that temperature can have a substantial impact on the mechanical
behavior of particle interactions. The temperature dependence of viscosity is one of
the most important variables for polymers, which is given by an Arrhenius type equa-
tion [6, 13]. As the temperature approaches higher values, nearing the melting point,
the particles within a stressed state experience a reduction in stiffness. Consequently,
this leads to increased deformation and larger overlaps between particles due to the
compressive forces acting upon them. Luding et al. [20] introduced a new discrete
model for the sintering of particulate materials with a temperature-dependent elastic
modulus.
  The role of particle shape coupled with its thermal properties is hardly ever
explored in the literature and is thus a subject with great potential. We propose
an extension of the DEM that incorporates heat transfer capabilities by combining a
multisphere algorithm with a thermal discrete particle model, thereby enabling the
simulation of non-spherical particles. To showcase the applicability of this model,
we conduct simulations of a powder spreading process utilizing irregularly shaped
Polyamide 12 (PA12) powder particles. This demonstration illustrates the effective-
ness of the proposed model in capturing the behavior of non-spherical particles in
real-world scenarios.
   Improving the quality of the layer during powder spreading can be achieved by
various means. In addition to exploring the thermal, cohesive, and overall mechanical
properties of the powder material itself, an optimization of the steps of the powder
application process can result in improved layer characteristics. To this end, the
efﬁciency of a vibrating recoating mechanism has been explored with respect to the
layer density and surface roughness.

The ﬁrst particle-based numerical tool was developed by Parteli [28] based on an

10.1 Powder packing density

The three PD sampling volumes and resulting PD values for the stable region of the powder

bed are shown in Figure 46.





Figure 46 PD in stable region of the simulated powder bed. A: measurement method 2 (PDminsim), B:
method 4 (PDmeasuredsim), C: method 3 (PDmaxsim).



As is seen from Figure 46, PD varies between 45-58 % depending on the measurement method.

Methods 2 and 3 were used for Figure 46 A and Figure 46 C respectively and yielded slightly

lower and higher values as was expected. The method 4 measurement from the stable region as

seen in Figure 46 B was considered the best representation of the PD measured from the

validation experiment, and thus its value needs to match the validation experiment to validate

the simulation. This measurement produced a PD value of 52 %, which matches that of the

validation experiment within one percentage point, and the simulation model can be considered

validated by PD. A tilted perspective view of PDmeasuredsim is provided in Figure 47.                                                                        85





Figure 47 Tilted view of PDmeasuredsim.


As shown in Figure 47, the top xy-plane is placed so that the area of cut particles and empty

space are approximately equal. Small variations in the plane location (i.e. variations that are

small enough to not be reasonably considered method 2 or 3 type measurements) had no more

than two percentage points difference in PD.

The simulation run was repeated with same parameters, and identical measurements were taken.

These resulted in identical PD values for PDminsim and PDmaxsim, while PDmeasuredsim was

53%, one percentage point higher than in the first run. It should be noted that the simulations

are not completely deterministic as the initial particle generation is randomised.

The same three PD sampling volumes and resulting PD values for the full length of the powder

bed are shown in Figure 48.





Figure 48 PD in entire length of the simulated powder bed. A: measurement method 2 (PDminsim), B:
method 4 (PDmeasuredsim), C: method 3 (PDmaxsim).                                                                        86


As is seen in Figure 48, the PD for the entire length is lower than for the stable region, as

expected. This is mostly likely due to the fact that the powder bed surface dips below the top

xy-plane of the sampling volume near the end of recoater travel, leaving more empty space in

the sampling volume. This is supported by the fact that the measurement using method 3 in

Figure 48 C has identical PD to the corresponding measurement in the stable region, while the

method 2 value in Figure 48 A is 8 percentage points lower compared to the stable region. For

the method 4 measurement in Figure 48 B, PD is three percentage points lower, likely caused

by the same lack or powder at the end of recoater travel. This indicates that using the full length

of the powder bed for PD measurements may yield low values, unless the powder dosing issue

can be solved. This is important since the validation experiment likely does not have a similar

issue due to the frontal location of the sampling area.

It should be noted that PD in simulation should not be higher than in validation, but there may

be reason to believe it can be lower than validation PD while being considered validated. This

is because intuitively PD should increase with the number of layers as the weight of the powder

compresses itself, and the simulation has an order of magnitude fewer layers than the validation.

In the repeated simulation run, values of PDminsim and PDmeasuredsim were two percentage

points higher (51% and 39% respectively) while PDmaxsim was unchanged (58%). The

sampling methods 2 and 4 (min and measured PD) are most affected by changes in powder bed

thickness, and the repeat run featured a visibly more uniform bed thickness. Therefore it can be

safely assumed there is little to no variance in actual packing structure between simulation runs,

though it is possible for the powder bed uniformity to change. It is recommended that in the

future when comparing simulation runs to each other (and not a validation experiment), the

measurement method 3 is used.

More details on the repeat simulation run are provided in Appendix 9.

10.2 Particle behaviour during recoating

In order to understand the particle packing behaviour, the entire recoating process was analysed

and PD was also measured from the powder dispenser as shown in Figure 49.                                                                        87





Figure 49 Compression in the dispenser before the recoater blade.


As seen in Figure 49, powder bulk in the dispenser is compressed in front of and under the

recoater blade and decompressed after the blade, indicating that the blade has a compressive

force on the powder bulk in the dispenser. PD measured from the white box is 95%, which

should be practically impossible, suggesting the compressive force is large enough to cause a

normally unallowed overlap between particles. However, it should be noted that the sampling

volume is completely embedded in the powder bulk, which increases the PD measurement

value by up to 10 percentage points compared to the likely true PD. The compression causing

an elastic overlap in the particles is also evident from the fact that there is an updraft or wave

of powder immediately following the blade as the powder decompresses and elastic force is

released. Such a degree of elasticity is unlikely to occur in real metallic particles, which means

that the spring constant may need its own calibration for future experiments. However, it is not

likely that this elasticity under compressive force affects packing in the powder bed, as the

particles are mostly deposited by gravity and not a significant normal force. Compressive force

in the dispenser is larger likely due to the blade impacting relatively deep into the mass of the

powder bulk.

Another effect of the blade impacting the powder bulk is the significant spray of particles seen

in Figure 50.                                                                        88





Figure 50 Finer particles being sprayed as the recoater contacts powder in the dispenser


As seen in Figure 50, small particles are sprayed far and wide as the blade enters the dispenser

for the first time. It is not known whether the spray phenomenon occurs in a real L-PBF process

as well, as the powder flow behaviour is not separately validated. It can be that this spray does

not exist in reality in the same scale due to VDW forces binding together the smallest particles,

which is not accounted for in this simulation.

Another interesting phenomenon seen in Figure 50 is the separation of small and large particles

in front of the blade. As the blade moves through the powder bulk, the smaller half of particles

seem to percolate to the top due to some internal flow in the powder bulk. A rotating flow or

vortex likely exists in front of the blade though, as large particles are eventually picked up as

well, as is seen in Figure 51. Similar vortex and compression phenomena were also observed

by Wu et al. (2022) [52].                                                                        89

10.3 Sources of uncertainty

Since the simulation is a representation of reality based on rough measurements and estimates,

there are always many uncertainties. Physical measurements always have error, though in a

simulation such as this the measurement error may be negligible compared to the error resulting

from  translating  the measurements  into  input  parameters, which  are  only  simplified

representations of the real physical properties that were measured. For example, the friction

coefficient of a particle is only a simplification of multiple physical phenomena; interlocking,

rolling resistance, adhesive forces, contaminant particles, and friction.                                                                        92


A parameter with a large effect on packing is the PSD. PSD is inputted as 10 size classes, which

is a very coarse approximation of the true PSD. Depending on which size classes are chosen

from the dynamic image analysis or laser diffraction data, the resulting input PSD may change

significantly. Also it should be decided whether to use a constant “resolution” of size classes or

focus on large, small, or mid-size classes, all of which affect packing behaviour differently.

Besides PSD, the particles are simplified in shape as well. Real particles feature defects and

may not be completely spherical. FLOW-3D only supports spherical particles for now, so an

effort was made to choose higher values of friction to emulate the rolling resistance of non-

spherical particles. The effect on PD of non-spherical particles compared to spherical particles

was found by Gao et al. (2020) [108] to be less than two percentage points, so it can be assumed

that error in PD arising from sphericity is not the main concern.

In this simulation work, many physical properties of the objects and particles are simplified to

a simple friction coefficient and a smooth surface. Some surfaces, like the backside of the blade,

are pixelated. The simulated powder bed is also a small sample of the real system with a higher

solid surface area to powder volume ratio, which may cause a pronounced wall effect in powder

packing; packing structures at the wall-powder interface are less dense than in bulk powder.

Many process features are also ignored in this simulation; for example, the real building

platform is moved down and up after each recoat, which may compact the powder. Also, the

powder is poured into the dispenser from higher altitude than in simulation, which may compact

it. Other vibrations during processing may also influence PD.

Besides parameters, there are uncertainties regarding the discrepancies between validation and

simulation. The powder bed thickness of the validation sample was about 20 times higher than

in the simulations which was only recoated four times. It could be assumed that a thicker powder

bed compresses under its own weight, increasing PD. Furthermore, measuring the exact volume

of the PD sampling volume in the validation sample is difficult and measurements often

featured up to 0.1 mm of deviation, though the PD values between samples were very uniform.

Also, applying the sampling volume measurement directly to the simulation is impossible. In

the validation sample, only the volume of the sample is measured, but mass of powder outside

the volume is also included in the PD calculations. For example, the powder bed may well be

taller than the built wall which is measured, in which case the measurement yields too high PD

values and cannot be exactly replicated in simulation.                                                                        93

11 Conclusions


EOS Finland aims to aid the development of Tungsten powder feedstock by computer

simulation. The goal of this thesis was to develop a simulation model of the powder bed

recoating process to act as a proof of concept and platform for future development of a more

comprehensive simulation model. Development of this preliminary simulation model would

also include its validation using a purpose-built validation experiment.

Literature on previous powder bed simulations and powder bed characterisation studies was

reviewed to compile information about the relevant powder bed parameters, calibration

methods, validation methods, and typical input values for material properties. Powder packing

density PD was found to be the most relevant powder bed parameter, and the best-suited

characterisation method was considered to be the “open cup” experiment. A variety of

calibration experiments were also found and their ideal use cases identified. All necessary

simulation input parameters were also available in literature.

An “open cup” validation experiment was developed based on findings in literature. In this

experiment, a thin wall enclosure is built with the L-PBF process, trapping a known volume

of powder inside the formed enclosure, or “cup”. The sampled powder is weighed enabling

the calculation of the powder packing density of the recoated powder bed, which is then

compared to the PD of the simulated powder bed.

The validation experiment was repeated five times. Measures were taken to reduce and

quantify error resulting from various stages of the process, and all the tested sources of error

were negligible. Average powder packing density characterised in the validation experiment

was 52 %, with a standard deviation of 0.2 %.

Input values for the simulation model were mostly characterised by rheometry, pycnometry,

dynamic image analysis. Calibration experiments were not implemented as they are time

consuming and unnecessary in this case; the powder was thoroughly characterised by the EOS

Finland laboratory and any unknown parameters were available in literature.

The simulation model featured a building platform of about 6 mm x 1.5 mm size.

Approximately 370 000 particles were generated in a dispenser, which was enough to recoat

the powder bed four times, with the first layer being of double height. After four recoats, the

simulation run ended and PD was measured with different methods and from both the full

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study develops a Bayesian optimization framework to calibrate two discrete element method (DEM) parameters—the cohesion-related surface energy coefficient (k) and the rolling resistance coefficient (μr)—based on experimental void ratio data obtained from powder consolidation tests. The optimized parameter set reproduces the void ratio obtained from the consolidation experiment, demonstrating efficient and physically plausible calibration under confined loading. However, when these parameters are applied to powder spreading simulations, the resulting powder beds become excessively cohesive, leading to poor layer uniformity. This discrepancy is attributed to (i) the mismatch in mechanical scaling (σ/E) between the experimental and simulated conditions and (ii) the shift in dominant particle-scale mechanics from normal-force-controlled consolidation to shear-dominated spreading. The results indicate that DEM parameter calibration for powder bed-based additive manufacturing should incorporate shear-related experimental metrics and scaling considerations rather than rely solely on consolidation-based fitting.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Digital Twins (DTs) are transforming manufacturing by bridging the physical and digital worlds, enabling real-time insights, predictive analytics, and enhanced decision making. In Industry 4.0, DTs facilitate automation and data integration, while Industry 5.0 emphasizes human-centric, resilient, and sustainable production. However, implementing DTs in robotic metal additive manufacturing (AM) remains challenging because of the complexity of the wire-based laser metal deposition (LMD) process, the need for real-time monitoring, and the demand for advanced defect detection to ensure high-quality prints. This work proposes a structured DT architecture for a robotic wire-based LMD cell, following a standard framework. Three DT implementations were developed. First, a real-time 3D simulation in RoboDK, integrated with a 2D Node-RED dashboard, enabled motion validation and live process monitoring via MQTT (message queuing telemetry transport) telemetry, minimizing toolpath errors and collisions. Second, an Industrial IoT-based system using KUKA iiQoT (Industrial Internet of Things Quality of Things) facilitated predictive maintenance by analyzing motor loads, joint temperatures, and energy consumption, allowing early anomaly detection and reducing unplanned downtime. Third, the Meltio dashboard provided real-time insights into the laser temperature, wire tension, and deposition accuracy, ensuring adaptive control based on live telemetry. Additionally, a prescriptive analytics layer leveraging historical data in FireStore was integrated to optimize the process performance, enabling data-driven decision making.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Finite element (FE)-based numerical approaches are widely used to simulate additive manufacturing processes and predict mechanical response, predefined meshes and repeated remeshing make it difficult to manage spatial resolution without adding complex computational overhead when simulating the path-following process. To address the challenges of mesh-dependent resolution, this study employs a bonded discrete element method (DEM) in which solids are represented as bonded particle assemblies whose bond network is defined by process parameters encoded in the toolpath and the discrete nature of the method allows for the direct representation of complex toolpath-induced internal architecture without frequent remeshing typically required in mesh-based approaches. Here, the additive manufacturing process is modeled as a sequence of G-code-driven particle deposition and bond-activation events, such that infill pattern, infill density, scan direction, and build orientation explicitly determine the resulting bond network. Firstly, we test the model’s capability in reflecting the effect of infill densities by using virtual three-point bending test by adjusting the bond’s parameters. Further, parametric studies are systematically conducted to investigate the coupled and individual influences of scan direction and build orientation across different infill configurations. It shows that the proposed method can reflect the changes in load-transfer paths, deformation localization, and sensitivity of bending stiffness to process parameters. These findings demonstrate that DEM-based virtual testing can link scan direction and build orientation to the elastic and flexural behavior of printed components, offering valuable guidance for developing additive manufacturing strategies.</jats:p>

The excerpt identifies the two calibrated DEM parameters as the cohesion-related surface energy coefficient k and rolling resistance coefficient µr. The reported explanations are a mismatch in mechanical scaling (σ/E) between experiment and simulation, and a change from normal-force-controlled consolidation to shear-dominated spreading. Consequently, the study argues that powder-bed AM calibration should include shear-sensitive experimental metrics and scaling considerations, rather than relying only on consolidation data. The excerpt does not provide software implementation details or state whether code, parameter files, or experimental/simulation data are publicly available; those points require the full article or supplementary/repository information. It characterizes Bayesian optimization as an efficient parameter-search/calibration strategy intended to minimize expensive DEM runs, contrasting it conceptually with exhaustive parameter sweeps. particle shape and thermal effects are of critical importance.
  The addition of vibrations during powder application was investigated via DEM
simulations with non-spherical, cohesive particles as a new application system. The
effect of vibration and process characteristics was explored. Small frequency and
amplitude, combined with small recoating velocity, lead to denser granular beds of
reduced porosity. Large frequency and amplitude, however, lead to a vibro-ﬂuidized
state of the particles and granular beds with loose conﬁguration characterized by an13 DEM Simulation of the Powder Application in Powder Bed Fusion                  281

increased porosity. For practical applications, the choice of frequency and amplitude
should be considered in combination with a speciﬁc translational velocity of the
recoating process.

2.2. Calibration of DEM Parameters

    For the DEM simulation of the spreading process, DEM parameters, including powder material
property parameters and contact model parameters, play a crucial role in getting the correct
results [26,27].
    The Al2O3 ceramic powders are widely used in AM processes [28–30]. In this work, Al2O3 ceramic
powders (Dongchao Technologies, Dongguan, China) are the research object. Particle size, density,
shear modulus, and Poisson’s ratio are the powder material property parameters. The particles size
and density are measured in order to calibrate the DEM parameters. A dynamic optical particle
analyzer measures the particle size (Retsch Camsizer X2, Retsch technology GmbH, Haan, Germany).
The particle size D (10), D (50), and D (90) are 24, 48, and 72 µm.  Particles density is measured
by a Gas Pycnometer (Bei Shi De Instrument-S & T, Beijing, China) with a value of 3820 kg/m3.
The micromorphology of powders is observed by secondary electron imaging in the scanning electron
microscope (SEM, Phenom ProX, Phenom-World, Eindhoven, Holland). Figure 1 shows the SEM
micrograph for Al2O3 ceramic powders around ball shape. The shear modulus and Poisson’s ratio are
drawn from reference literature [31]. According to the literature [32], Young’s modulus has little eﬀect
on the simulation results. The value of Young’s modulus is set as 3 GPa, which is decreased two orders
of magnitude than the actual value in order to reduce computer time consumption.

Zhang et al. specifically investigate roller-spreading parameters and powder-bed density. A novel apparatus for the simulation of powder spreading procedures in powder-bed-based additive manufacturing processes: design, calibration, and case study. Journal of Manufacturing and Materials Processing, 7:135, Jul 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jmmp7040135, doi:10.3390/jmmp7040135. This article has 14 citations.

This excerpt provides direct evidence that LAMMPS was used as the DEM software for all simulations. It does not mention MercuryDPM or LIGGGHTS, nor does it discuss open-source coupling through CFDEM or OpenFOAM, or comparisons with commercial packages such as EDEM, Fluent, or FLOW-3D. The study uses a multi-sphere representation of initially rod-shaped particles. Aspect ratios of 1.5, 2.0, and 2.5 are modeled with 2, 3, and 4 spheroids, respectively; the authors explicitly state that this reduces computational costs. The contact interaction is represented by a linear Hookean spring-dashpot model, selected for its low computational cost. The excerpt also cautions that absolute parameter values depend on powder properties, particle shape, and size distribution, indicating that model outcomes may be sensitive to particle-scale representation and physical-property assumptions. Negar Sani, Johannes Quist, Sofia Kazi, Gowtham Soundarapandiyan, Gustav Kettil, Laura Cordova, Eduard Hryha, and Fredrik Edelvik. Efficient dem calibration of am powders using a rotating drum through froude number scaling. Progress in Additive Manufacturing, 11:5411-5425, Apr 2026. The excerpt provides evidence relevant to cost-saving geometric scaling in DEM, but it does not identify coating DEM software, public input files, datasets, the Haeri dataset DOI, or open-source/commercial coupling frameworks. The study reduces the rotating-particulate-analysis drum diameter by a 1:5 ratio for simulation and adjusts angular velocity to preserve the Froude number. For comparison between experiments and simulations, energy is normalized by drum radius and time by the rotation period. The authors also test the scaling approach using three additional simulations with different drum radii, which supports evaluating whether drum-size reduction preserves the relevant response. This is useful evidence for reduced computational cost through geometry scaling, although the excerpt gives no runtime, particle-count, or cost comparison. The passage concerns calibration of Inconel 718 and Ti64 powders and reports that calibrated interaction parameters remain within literature ranges. It describes powder-specific sensitivity: Inconel 718 is more influenced by sliding friction, while Ti64 is more sensitive to surface energy and cohesive interactions. However, it does not discuss particle-size upscaling, coarse-graining, or the effect of changing particle diameter or number independently of drum geometry. From text 'goh2026bookofabstracts pages 31-33'.

WP Goh, C Hare, and M Ghadiri. Book of abstracts: past, present and future of particle technology conference 2026. Unknown journal, 2026.

The excerpt provides relevant evidence concerning DEM–CFD modelling, computational savings through particle coarse-graining, and sensitivity to particle upscaling. The study uses FELMI, described as an in-house DEM–CFD solver, coupled with a signed-distance-function immersed-boundary method for moving and arbitrarily shaped walls, coarse-grained DEM for reducing particle numbers, and a rotational-resistance model for representing nonspherical particle effects with spherical computational particles. The coarse-grained approach represents multiple original particles by one computational particle while maintaining energy consistency and substantially reducing computational cost. Validation in a linear shoe–die filling system found excellent agreement between original-particle and coarse-grained simulations. However, simply enlarging particles by three times their original diameter produced markedly different macroscopic filling behaviour, specifically faster filling attributed to reduced air-drag effects. This directly supports the need for sensitivity checks when scaling particle geometry or using computationally enlarged particles. The excerpt does not identify MercuryDPM, LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS, CFDEM, OpenFOAM, EDEM, Fluent, FLOW-3D, or the Haeri dataset/DOI, and therefore supplies no evidence about those software packages, open-source versus commercial licensing, publicly accessible inputs, or dataset availability.

MJ Mohammed. Discrete element method in pharmaceutical engineering: a critical review of powder processing, tablet manufacturing, and pulmonary drug delivery. Unknown journal, Unknown year.

The excerpt provides evidence relevant to cost-saving geometry simplification and sensitivity to particle upscaling, but it does not identify specific DEM software packages, datasets, or coupling frameworks. It states that industrial-scale modelling commonly requires simplified particle shapes, narrowed size distributions, or coarse-grained parcels because representing every physical particle is often impractical. Spherical particles reduce computational expense, whereas clumps and other non-spherical representations improve representation of interlocking and rotational resistance at greater computational cost. The review cautions that coarse graining is not dynamically neutral: it can alter contact number, mass scaling, cohesion, and segregation behaviour. Therefore, an upscaled model must be recalibrated and independently validated rather than assumed equivalent to the original powder. The excerpt also notes that explicit DEM becomes expensive for finer or stiffer particles because the time step must remain small relative to contact dynamics. Calibration should use bulk tests and reflect the intended process regime; multi-objective calibration is preferable where possible. No evidence is supplied here for MercuryDPM, LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS, a Haeri dataset DOI, CFDEM/OpenFOAM, or comparisons with commercial EDEM, Fluent, or FLOW-3D.

{"answer": "# Physics-based prediction of powder-bed spreadability

**Bottom line.** Particle-resolved discrete-element modelling (DEM) is the best-supported way to predict *how a specified powder, recoater and operating condition* produce a bed. It can resolve coverage gaps, local packing, roughness and size segregation that a bulk-flow number cannot. Its predictions still require independent spreading measurements: fitting a powder to a doser, shear cell or consolidation test does not establish that its contact parameters transfer to a thin, rapidly sheared layer. A published Bayesian-optimization study reproduced consolidation yet produced an excessively cohesive bed when its parameters were transferred to spreading. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000043)

## Models, outputs and validation

In **blade or rake DEM**, particles move through a prescribed clearance under gravity, particle–particle and particle–wall forces. In **roller DEM**, traverse speed, rotation, roller diameter and gap additionally control compaction, jamming and shear. Common choices are Hertz–Mindlin normal/tangential contact, Coulomb sliding, a rolling-resistance torque and an adhesive law; published spreading models use either JKR adhesion or simplified JKR (SJKR). These are *different parameterizations*: an SJKR cohesion-energy-density value should not be interpreted as a JKR surface energy or an intrinsic material constant. Spheres efficiently represent near-spherical atomized alloys; bonded multisphere clumps better represent irregular or satellite-bearing particles at greater cost. Fouda and Bayly’s idealized blade study isolates shear dilation before and within the gap and inertial dilation after deposition: increasing blade speed decreased packing, whereas increasing the gap raised it. Roller studies likewise found layer thickness and traverse speed consequential, but their conclusions depend on the powder and recoater geometry. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000060)

For comparison across simulations, define **local packing fraction** as solid particle volume divided by a *specified sampling volume*, **void fraction** as one minus that fraction, and **areal loading** as deposited mass divided by sampled area. Also report deposited height and its distribution, substrate **coverage** or uncovered-area fraction from registered images, surface-height roughness such as *Sa*, and species-resolved particle-size/composition maps along and across spreading. These observables are not interchangeable: a smooth surface does not establish a dense interior. Include the sampling depth, treatment of particles crossing its boundary, edge exclusions and number of layers with every reported packing value. Lee et al. assessed height, packing, roughness and size redistribution; binder-jet experiments demonstrate why directional segregation and local density must also be measured. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000031)

The following comparison separates direct experimental agreement from simulation-to-simulation benchmarking and unvalidated model possibilities. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000058)

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**The strongest numerical validation found illustrates a measurement hazard.** In an Alloy 718 LPBF open-cup experiment, five samples gave **52.4% mean packing fraction**, with **0.20 percentage-point standard deviation**. A four-layer DEM result was **52%** using a corresponding central sampling region. Merely changing the simulated sampling-volume definition yielded **45%, 52% or 58%**; sampling the entire bed rather than its stable central region also changed the answer. Thus, agreement to within a percentage point is meaningful only when experimental and simulated volumes are constructed alike. The cropped density-window comparison makes this dependence visible. Lee et al. independently reported recoated-bed height within **1%** of experiment, alongside qualitative agreement in pile motion, rather than a comparably precise experimental confirmation of every simulated packing or segregation output. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000036)

**Across processes.** Binder-jetting DEM uses the same dry recoating mechanics but particularly needs spatial packing and composition because these determine binder access and green-part heterogeneity. In a 5/20 µm alumina mixture, simulated and observed segregation both placed more fines early in the spreading direction and coarser particles later; the measured bed-packing decline along that direction was **7.65%**, but a point-by-point numerical DEM error was not established. For electron-beam powder-bed fusion, a study of reused feedstock simulated rake coverage and packing for spherical and irregular multisphere particles; it found poorly covered thin layers and shape-dependent jamming. Its recoating agreement was not reported as a numerical error. EBM also warrants process-specific temperature and powder-state validation rather than assuming ambient LPBF parameters transfer. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000057)

**Coupling and acceleration have narrower evidence.** A metal binder-jet study first made a 17-4PH bed with LIGGGHTS DEM, then passed fixed particle geometry to a finite-volume, volume-of-fluid simulation of liquid-binder wetting and penetration, checking the workflow against single-layer printing experiments. This is *sequential DEM → CFD*, not a demonstrated two-way gas–particle CFD–DEM predictor of recoating. Two-way CFD–DEM is appropriate when carrier-gas drag or gas-driven entrainment matters; liquid infiltration requires wetting and capillarity, not merely a gas-drag correction. Neither should be added to an ambient dry-recoating model without an experimentally motivated fluid effect. (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000033)

Coarse-grained DEM reduces particle count but changes the ratios among gravity, cohesion, contact forces and fluid drag unless its scaling rules preserve them. An industrial **shoe-filling**, *not AM recoating*, DEM–CFD example retained macroscopic behavior with a calibrated coarse-grained model, whereas simply tripling particle diameter made filling faster because air drag changed. Geometry reduction without enlarging particles is a different compromise: Sani et al. retained the real alloy size distribution in a rotating-drum calibration, reduced drum radius fivefold and adjusted speed to preserve Froude number. They explicitly did **not** establish that a drum-calibrated response predicts recoating. Continuum granular-flow, finite-volume or material-point formulations can represent averaged stresses, solids fraction and a moving free surface at larger scale; in the retrieved studies, however, there was **no independently quantified validation of a continuum recoater model** for fine-layer coverage gaps, roughness and segregation. These approaches are candidates for larger, well-resolved regions or hybrids, not a demonstrated replacement for particle-resolved thin-layer DEM. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000029)

## Do conventional flow tests predict spreadability?

**Not reliably as universal rankings.** Hall/Carney discharge interrogates an orifice and can return *no flow* for powder that a recoater can spread; angle of repose depends on its formation protocol; Hausner ratio reflects tapping rather than the weak confinement and shearing of recoating. Shear-cell flow function, *ffc*, depends on consolidation stress and usefully constrains yield behavior, but a value measured under substantial consolidation is not itself a prediction of a thin layer. FT4 blade energy and rotating-drum avalanching probe more dynamic states, yet their ability to rank powders remains conditional on test protocol, material and spreader. Use B213/B964, B212/B527, D7891/D6773, repose, sieving/laser diffraction and loss on drying as **independent characterization**, not interchangeable measures of spreading quality. For D6773 or FT4 shear, retain the full stress-dependent yield locus and wall-friction information where possible rather than reducing everything to one *ffc*. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000049)

Two experiments show the distinction particularly clearly. Spierings et al. found that the Hausner ratio failed to track their **optical powder-flowability classification**, whereas a fitted combination of drum avalanche/surface descriptors achieved **R² = 0.94** against *that optical rating*. This is **not** an R² for measured recoated-layer packing or roughness. In a later **27-condition, 405-layer** comparison of 316L, Alloy 718 and AlSi10Mg across blade, roller and hopper recoaters at 50, 150 and 250 mm/s, Brocksieper et al. found significant powder × recoater × speed interactions in measured layer *Sa*. Alloy 718 did **not flow in the Hall funnel** yet could make blade/roller layers as smooth as, or smoother than, the more freely flowing 316L; AlSi10Mg gave the roughest layers, a ranking most conventional flow results did not anticipate. FT4 **specific energy** indicated its poorer behavior. Drum avalanche and dynamic angles did **not** correlate with observed application behavior in that study, although speed-dependent drum cohesive-index trends resembled **blade** roughness trends for powders already characterized. The authors explicitly did **not** establish prediction for an unknown powder or for roller/hopper systems. They measured surface roughness, **not bed density**. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000048)

Accordingly, evaluate each conventional test against an actual, held-out spreading endpoint—coverage, *Sa*, areal mass or packing—**separately for each recoater and speed regime**. A significant within-alloy or within-machine association is useful screening evidence, not a transferable material law. (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000008)

## Open implementations and reproducibility

- **LIGGGHTS-PUBLIC 3.8.0** is directly relevant to the existing doser: Katagiri et al. publish a model specification using Hertz–Mindlin, `sjkr2` cohesion and `cdt` rolling resistance; Sang et al. use open-source LIGGGHTS for binder-jet bed generation. The published parameter table and equations are useful *starting descriptions*, **not a verified downloadable runnable recoater input deck** or transferable parameters. In particular, changing from constant-directional-torque rolling resistance to another rolling law requires recalibration. (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000025)
- **LAMMPS** was used for Haeri’s blade-profile and multisphere recoating simulations; **MercuryDPM** and **YADE** are documented open granular-simulation packages that can serve as alternative modelling bases. The evidence retrieved does not establish a specific maintained, ready-to-run AM recoating example for each. **EDEM, ANSYS Fluent and FLOW-3D** appear in relevant studies but should not be represented as open-source substitutes. Check the version, license and implemented adhesion/rolling-law definitions before porting any deck. (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035)
- A **published simulation dataset** is explicitly cited as Haeri, *Dataset—discrete element simulation of powder spreading in additive manufacturing* (2016), **DOI: 10.15129/c5993a8f-812d-46cf-bef5-92e985d12446**. The retrieved publication does **not** establish that this deposit includes the complete geometry, scripts, executable input deck and contact-law implementation needed for one-command reproduction. Haeri’s 2017 paper publishes geometry and contact-model details, and Sani et al. report supplementary experimental drum-energy series; neither fact alone verifies a runnable recoating deck. No fully verified downloadable open-source *recoating input deck* was located in the reviewed sources. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000059)

## Recommended doser-to-spreader calibration experiment

1. **Separate measured particle properties from inferred effective contacts.** For each powder, measure particle skeletal density, number/volume size distributions, morphology, water content and controlled relative humidity; record PLA/PETG surface condition and powder history. Set DEM size and density from these measurements. Infer *effective model-specific* particle–particle and particle–wall adhesion, sliding and rolling parameters, rather than claiming that a uniquely inferred `sjkr2` coefficient is intrinsic cohesion. The need to account for shape, adhesion and particle-size distribution in packing has experimental DEM support. (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000049)
2. **Calibrate against several distinct features, not salt throughput alone.** Use replicated mass/revolution versus tilt and rpm, per-tap released mass, stop-afterflow curves and zero-flow increments with their uncertainty; include fill level, initialization and wall/material state as inputs. A practical *proposed* likelihood uses a continuous error model for mass and afterflow, a Bernoulli/binomial model for no-flow events, and a separate tap-response component. Treat cohesion–rolling-friction and wall-friction–packing trade-offs as identifiability questions. The observed **105 mg/rev** salt match without fitted parameters is an excellent forward check, but cannot identify the contact parameters of the other 12 powders. A published consolidation-only calibration provides a concrete warning about transfer to shear-dominated spreading. (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000043)
3. **Make posterior inference computationally feasible, and distinguish it from Bayesian optimization.** At **26–30 CPU-min per revolution**, 100 full-revolution evaluations cost approximately **43–50 CPU-hours**, before replication or multiple operating points. First screen parameters with a reduced, demonstrably representative outlet or experimental design; fit a multi-output emulator with predictive uncertainty, adaptively acquire additional DEM runs, and then sample a posterior that includes measurement noise and simulator discrepancy. Check the posterior against reserved tilt/speed/tap conditions and direct shear/density measurements. Bayesian *optimization* of a squared-error objective, as published for consolidation, finds candidate point estimates; it does not by itself deliver posterior uncertainty. Geometry-downscaled drum calibration may save cost, but particle enlargement or altered tool-gap/particle-size ratio must be independently tested before using it for the approximately 3 mm outlet or micron-scale recoater gap. (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000053, pqac-00000059)
4. **Test transfer in a separate spreading rig.** For gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047 first, measure blade and roller layers at several clearances and traverse speeds under controlled humidity. Register optical coverage and profilometric *Sa* with weighed areal loading and a trapped-volume/open-cup packing measurement; map PSD or composition along the travel direction for mixtures. Compare *posterior-predicted distributions* with held-out layers, not just a calibrated mean. Extend to irregular silicon grades and deliberately different sizes only after checking shape and cohesion-model adequacy. A doser fingerprint may be a useful prior or screening feature, but **its predictive value for recoating remains to be demonstrated**, especially because the doser’s tapping and wall contacts differ from blade/roller shear. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000037)"}
