{"answer": "# Physics-based prediction of powder-bed spreadability

**Bottom line.** Particle-resolved discrete-element modelling (DEM) is the best-supported way to predict *how a specified powder, recoater and operating condition* produce a bed. It can resolve coverage gaps, local packing, roughness and size segregation that a bulk-flow number cannot. Its predictions still require independent spreading measurements: fitting a powder to a doser, shear cell or consolidation test does not establish that its contact parameters transfer to a thin, rapidly sheared layer. A published Bayesian-optimization study reproduced consolidation yet produced an excessively cohesive bed when its parameters were transferred to spreading. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000043)

## Models, outputs and validation

In **blade or rake DEM**, particles move through a prescribed clearance under gravity, particle–particle and particle–wall forces. In **roller DEM**, traverse speed, rotation, roller diameter and gap additionally control compaction, jamming and shear. Common choices are Hertz–Mindlin normal/tangential contact, Coulomb sliding, a rolling-resistance torque and an adhesive law; published spreading models use either JKR adhesion or simplified JKR (SJKR). These are *different parameterizations*: an SJKR cohesion-energy-density value should not be interpreted as a JKR surface energy or an intrinsic material constant. Spheres efficiently represent near-spherical atomized alloys; bonded multisphere clumps better represent irregular or satellite-bearing particles at greater cost. Fouda and Bayly’s idealized blade study isolates shear dilation before and within the gap and inertial dilation after deposition: increasing blade speed decreased packing, whereas increasing the gap raised it. Roller studies likewise found layer thickness and traverse speed consequential, but their conclusions depend on the powder and recoater geometry. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000060)

For comparison across simulations, define **local packing fraction** as solid particle volume divided by a *specified sampling volume*, **void fraction** as one minus that fraction, and **areal loading** as deposited mass divided by sampled area. Also report deposited height and its distribution, substrate **coverage** or uncovered-area fraction from registered images, surface-height roughness such as *Sa*, and species-resolved particle-size/composition maps along and across spreading. These observables are not interchangeable: a smooth surface does not establish a dense interior. Include the sampling depth, treatment of particles crossing its boundary, edge exclusions and number of layers with every reported packing value. Lee et al. assessed height, packing, roughness and size redistribution; binder-jet experiments demonstrate why directional segregation and local density must also be measured. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000031)

The following comparison separates direct experimental agreement from simulation-to-simulation benchmarking and unvalidated model possibilities. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000058)

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**The strongest numerical validation found illustrates a measurement hazard.** In an Alloy 718 LPBF open-cup experiment, five samples gave **52.4% mean packing fraction**, with **0.20 percentage-point standard deviation**. A four-layer DEM result was **52%** using a corresponding central sampling region. Merely changing the simulated sampling-volume definition yielded **45%, 52% or 58%**; sampling the entire bed rather than its stable central region also changed the answer. Thus, agreement to within a percentage point is meaningful only when experimental and simulated volumes are constructed alike. The cropped density-window comparison makes this dependence visible. Lee et al. independently reported recoated-bed height within **1%** of experiment, alongside qualitative agreement in pile motion, rather than a comparably precise experimental confirmation of every simulated packing or segregation output. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000036)

**Across processes.** Binder-jetting DEM uses the same dry recoating mechanics but particularly needs spatial packing and composition because these determine binder access and green-part heterogeneity. In a 5/20 µm alumina mixture, simulated and observed segregation both placed more fines early in the spreading direction and coarser particles later; the measured bed-packing decline along that direction was **7.65%**, but a point-by-point numerical DEM error was not established. For electron-beam powder-bed fusion, a study of reused feedstock simulated rake coverage and packing for spherical and irregular multisphere particles; it found poorly covered thin layers and shape-dependent jamming. Its recoating agreement was not reported as a numerical error. EBM also warrants process-specific temperature and powder-state validation rather than assuming ambient LPBF parameters transfer. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000057)

**Coupling and acceleration have narrower evidence.** A metal binder-jet study first made a 17-4PH bed with LIGGGHTS DEM, then passed fixed particle geometry to a finite-volume, volume-of-fluid simulation of liquid-binder wetting and penetration, checking the workflow against single-layer printing experiments. This is *sequential DEM → CFD*, not a demonstrated two-way gas–particle CFD–DEM predictor of recoating. Two-way CFD–DEM is appropriate when carrier-gas drag or gas-driven entrainment matters; liquid infiltration requires wetting and capillarity, not merely a gas-drag correction. Neither should be added to an ambient dry-recoating model without an experimentally motivated fluid effect. (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000033)

Coarse-grained DEM reduces particle count but changes the ratios among gravity, cohesion, contact forces and fluid drag unless its scaling rules preserve them. An industrial **shoe-filling**, *not AM recoating*, DEM–CFD example retained macroscopic behavior with a calibrated coarse-grained model, whereas simply tripling particle diameter made filling faster because air drag changed. Geometry reduction without enlarging particles is a different compromise: Sani et al. retained the real alloy size distribution in a rotating-drum calibration, reduced drum radius fivefold and adjusted speed to preserve Froude number. They explicitly did **not** establish that a drum-calibrated response predicts recoating. Continuum granular-flow, finite-volume or material-point formulations can represent averaged stresses, solids fraction and a moving free surface at larger scale; in the retrieved studies, however, there was **no independently quantified validation of a continuum recoater model** for fine-layer coverage gaps, roughness and segregation. These approaches are candidates for larger, well-resolved regions or hybrids, not a demonstrated replacement for particle-resolved thin-layer DEM. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000029)

## Do conventional flow tests predict spreadability?

**Not reliably as universal rankings.** Hall/Carney discharge interrogates an orifice and can return *no flow* for powder that a recoater can spread; angle of repose depends on its formation protocol; Hausner ratio reflects tapping rather than the weak confinement and shearing of recoating. Shear-cell flow function, *ffc*, depends on consolidation stress and usefully constrains yield behavior, but a value measured under substantial consolidation is not itself a prediction of a thin layer. FT4 blade energy and rotating-drum avalanching probe more dynamic states, yet their ability to rank powders remains conditional on test protocol, material and spreader. Use B213/B964, B212/B527, D7891/D6773, repose, sieving/laser diffraction and loss on drying as **independent characterization**, not interchangeable measures of spreading quality. For D6773 or FT4 shear, retain the full stress-dependent yield locus and wall-friction information where possible rather than reducing everything to one *ffc*. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000049)

Two experiments show the distinction particularly clearly. Spierings et al. found that the Hausner ratio failed to track their **optical powder-flowability classification**, whereas a fitted combination of drum avalanche/surface descriptors achieved **R² = 0.94** against *that optical rating*. This is **not** an R² for measured recoated-layer packing or roughness. In a later **27-condition, 405-layer** comparison of 316L, Alloy 718 and AlSi10Mg across blade, roller and hopper recoaters at 50, 150 and 250 mm/s, Brocksieper et al. found significant powder × recoater × speed interactions in measured layer *Sa*. Alloy 718 did **not flow in the Hall funnel** yet could make blade/roller layers as smooth as, or smoother than, the more freely flowing 316L; AlSi10Mg gave the roughest layers, a ranking most conventional flow results did not anticipate. FT4 **specific energy** indicated its poorer behavior. Drum avalanche and dynamic angles did **not** correlate with observed application behavior in that study, although speed-dependent drum cohesive-index trends resembled **blade** roughness trends for powders already characterized. The authors explicitly did **not** establish prediction for an unknown powder or for roller/hopper systems. They measured surface roughness, **not bed density**. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000048)

Accordingly, evaluate each conventional test against an actual, held-out spreading endpoint—coverage, *Sa*, areal mass or packing—**separately for each recoater and speed regime**. A significant within-alloy or within-machine association is useful screening evidence, not a transferable material law. (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000008)

## Open implementations and reproducibility

- **LIGGGHTS-PUBLIC 3.8.0** is directly relevant to the existing doser: Katagiri et al. publish a model specification using Hertz–Mindlin, `sjkr2` cohesion and `cdt` rolling resistance; Sang et al. use open-source LIGGGHTS for binder-jet bed generation. The published parameter table and equations are useful *starting descriptions*, **not a verified downloadable runnable recoater input deck** or transferable parameters. In particular, changing from constant-directional-torque rolling resistance to another rolling law requires recalibration. (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000025)
- **LAMMPS** was used for Haeri’s blade-profile and multisphere recoating simulations; **MercuryDPM** and **YADE** are documented open granular-simulation packages that can serve as alternative modelling bases. The evidence retrieved does not establish a specific maintained, ready-to-run AM recoating example for each. **EDEM, ANSYS Fluent and FLOW-3D** appear in relevant studies but should not be represented as open-source substitutes. Check the version, license and implemented adhesion/rolling-law definitions before porting any deck. (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035)
- A **published simulation dataset** is explicitly cited as Haeri, *Dataset—discrete element simulation of powder spreading in additive manufacturing* (2016), **DOI: 10.15129/c5993a8f-812d-46cf-bef5-92e985d12446**. The retrieved publication does **not** establish that this deposit includes the complete geometry, scripts, executable input deck and contact-law implementation needed for one-command reproduction. Haeri’s 2017 paper publishes geometry and contact-model details, and Sani et al. report supplementary experimental drum-energy series; neither fact alone verifies a runnable recoating deck. No fully verified downloadable open-source *recoating input deck* was located in the reviewed sources. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000059)

## Recommended doser-to-spreader calibration experiment

1. **Separate measured particle properties from inferred effective contacts.** For each powder, measure particle skeletal density, number/volume size distributions, morphology, water content and controlled relative humidity; record PLA/PETG surface condition and powder history. Set DEM size and density from these measurements. Infer *effective model-specific* particle–particle and particle–wall adhesion, sliding and rolling parameters, rather than claiming that a uniquely inferred `sjkr2` coefficient is intrinsic cohesion. The need to account for shape, adhesion and particle-size distribution in packing has experimental DEM support. (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000049)
2. **Calibrate against several distinct features, not salt throughput alone.** Use replicated mass/revolution versus tilt and rpm, per-tap released mass, stop-afterflow curves and zero-flow increments with their uncertainty; include fill level, initialization and wall/material state as inputs. A practical *proposed* likelihood uses a continuous error model for mass and afterflow, a Bernoulli/binomial model for no-flow events, and a separate tap-response component. Treat cohesion–rolling-friction and wall-friction–packing trade-offs as identifiability questions. The observed **105 mg/rev** salt match without fitted parameters is an excellent forward check, but cannot identify the contact parameters of the other 12 powders. A published consolidation-only calibration provides a concrete warning about transfer to shear-dominated spreading. (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000043)
3. **Make posterior inference computationally feasible, and distinguish it from Bayesian optimization.** At **26–30 CPU-min per revolution**, 100 full-revolution evaluations cost approximately **43–50 CPU-hours**, before replication or multiple operating points. First screen parameters with a reduced, demonstrably representative outlet or experimental design; fit a multi-output emulator with predictive uncertainty, adaptively acquire additional DEM runs, and then sample a posterior that includes measurement noise and simulator discrepancy. Check the posterior against reserved tilt/speed/tap conditions and direct shear/density measurements. Bayesian *optimization* of a squared-error objective, as published for consolidation, finds candidate point estimates; it does not by itself deliver posterior uncertainty. Geometry-downscaled drum calibration may save cost, but particle enlargement or altered tool-gap/particle-size ratio must be independently tested before using it for the approximately 3 mm outlet or micron-scale recoater gap. (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000053, pqac-00000059)
4. **Test transfer in a separate spreading rig.** For gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047 first, measure blade and roller layers at several clearances and traverse speeds under controlled humidity. Register optical coverage and profilometric *Sa* with weighed areal loading and a trapped-volume/open-cup packing measurement; map PSD or composition along the travel direction for mixtures. Compare *posterior-predicted distributions* with held-out layers, not just a calibrated mean. Extend to irregular silicon grades and deliberately different sizes only after checking shape and cohesion-model adequacy. A doser fingerprint may be a useful prior or screening feature, but **its predictive value for recoating remains to be demonstrated**, especially because the doser’s tapping and wall contacts differ from blade/roller shear. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000037)"}

state.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. What physics-based simulations are used to predict powder spreadability and packing in powder-bed additive manufacturing (laser powder bed fusion, binder jetting, electron beam melting): DEM of blade and roller recoating with cohesive contact models, coarse-grained DEM, coupled DEM-CFD, and continuum models? Which spreadability metrics (packing fraction, surface roughness, coverage, mass per area, void fraction, segregation) are computed, how are they validated against spreading experiments, and how well do standard flowability tests (Hall flow, angle of repose, Hausner ratio, shear-cell ffc, FT4 energy, avalanche angle in a rotating drum) predict spreadability? Which open-source codes and published input decks exist?

# Physics-based prediction of powder-bed spreadability

**Bottom line.** Particle-resolved discrete-element modelling (DEM) is the best-supported way to predict *how a specified powder, recoater and operating condition* produce a bed. It can resolve coverage gaps, local packing, roughness and size segregation that a bulk-flow number cannot. Its predictions still require independent spreading measurements: fitting a powder to a doser, shear cell or consolidation test does not establish that its contact parameters transfer to a thin, rapidly sheared layer. A published Bayesian-optimization study reproduced consolidation yet produced an excessively cohesive bed when its parameters were transferred to spreading. (fouda2019ademstudy pages 1-2, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 1-2, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 14-15)

## Models, outputs and validation

In **blade or rake DEM**, particles move through a prescribed clearance under gravity, particle–particle and particle–wall forces. In **roller DEM**, traverse speed, rotation, roller diameter and gap additionally control compaction, jamming and shear. Common choices are Hertz–Mindlin normal/tangential contact, Coulomb sliding, a rolling-resistance torque and an adhesive law; published spreading models use either JKR adhesion or simplified JKR (SJKR). These are *different parameterizations*: an SJKR cohesion-energy-density value should not be interpreted as a JKR surface energy or an intrinsic material constant. Spheres efficiently represent near-spherical atomized alloys; bonded multisphere clumps better represent irregular or satellite-bearing particles at greater cost. Fouda and Bayly’s idealized blade study isolates shear dilation before and within the gap and inertial dilation after deposition: increasing blade speed decreased packing, whereas increasing the gap raised it. Roller studies likewise found layer thickness and traverse speed consequential, but their conclusions depend on the powder and recoater geometry. (fouda2019ademstudy pages 1-2, zhang2020discreteelementsimulation pages 3-5, angelidakis2025demsimulationof pages 1-4, brika2023anovelapparatus pages 3-5)

For comparison across simulations, define **local packing fraction** as solid particle volume divided by a *specified sampling volume*, **void fraction** as one minus that fraction, and **areal loading** as deposited mass divided by sampled area. Also report deposited height and its distribution, substrate **coverage** or uncovered-area fraction from registered images, surface-height roughness such as *Sa*, and species-resolved particle-size/composition maps along and across spreading. These observables are not interchangeable: a smooth surface does not establish a dense interior. Include the sampling depth, treatment of particles crossing its boundary, edge exclusions and number of layers with every reported packing value. Lee et al. assessed height, packing, roughness and size redistribution; binder-jet experiments demonstrate why directional segregation and local density must also be measured. (lee2020effectofparticle pages 1-2, lee2020effectofparticle pages 9-11, brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 9-10, shahed2025powderspreadingbehavior pages 10-11)

The following comparison separates direct experimental agreement from simulation-to-simulation benchmarking and unvalidated model possibilities. (lee2020effectofparticle pages 9-11, haapa2023validationofpowder pages 7-9, qabani2026discreteelementanalysis pages 7-9)

| Model/process and study | Predicted or observed layer metrics | Validation | Essential limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LPBF, particle-resolved blade DEM — Haapa et al. (2023)** | Packing density, layer thickness, coverage and PSD segregation. Central stable-region density was **52%**; changing the sampling-volume definition changed it from **45% to 58%**. | Open-cup Alloy 718 experiment measured **52.4% ± 0.20 percentage points**, agreeing with the analogous 52% simulation result. | Apparent accuracy is strongly ROI-dependent; only four layers and spherical particles were modeled, and randomized initialization shifted the analogous density from 52% to 53%. (haapa2023validationofpowder pages 7-9, haapa2023simulationofmetalb pages 84-89, haapa2023validationofpowder media 7454531e) |
| **LPBF, multilayer rake DEM — Lee et al. (2020)** | Bed height, packing density, roughness, dynamic angle of repose, PSD and segregation; fivefold higher rake speed reduced simulated density by about **5%**. | Predicted bed height was within **1%** of experiment; pile evolution and later dynamic-angle variation agreed qualitatively. | Initial dynamic-angle discrepancy was attributed to unmodeled moisture/cohesive effects; packing-density validation was not comparably quantified. (lee2020effectofparticle pages 9-11) |
| **Blade versus roller DEM — Haeri (2017)** | Solid volume fraction and surface roughness for nonspherical particles; optimized blade reached roller-like packing and up to **2% higher** volume fraction at higher tested speeds. | Primarily comparative simulation; realistic multisphere shapes were used, with an associated public simulation dataset. | Results depend on simplified contact mechanics and shape representation; a complete runnable input deck was not verified. (brika2023anovelapparatus pages 11-12, brika2023anovelapparatus pages 3-5) |
| **Roller DEM — Zhang et al. (2020)** | Powder-bed density versus traverse speed, roller rotation, diameter and layer thickness; larger thickness and diameter improved density, while higher traverse speed degraded it. | Friction was measured by ASTM D6773; surface energy was calibrated to repose/avalanche behavior. A later reproduction reported **5.6% mean relative error** against Zhang’s density results. | This is cross-study reproduction rather than direct machine-scale validation; Young’s modulus was reduced by two orders of magnitude. (zhang2020discreteelementsimulation pages 3-5, qabani2026discreteelementanalysis pages 7-9) |
| **Binder jetting, roller DEM plus experiment — Shahed et al. (2025)** | Directional size segregation and packing: 5 µm particles accumulated near the start and 20 µm particles toward the trailing edge; packing density dropped **7.65%** along the spreading direction. | Simulation and experiment agreed on the **direction** of segregation and density gradient; no numerical DEM–experiment error was reported. | Directional agreement is not a quantitatively validated packing prediction; binder impact subsequently rearranged or ejected particles. (shahed2025powderspreadingbehavior pages 10-11) |
| **Binder jetting, irregular raw-sediment roller DEM — Al Qabani et al. (2026)** | Local and mean packing density, density variability and segregation using reconstructed multisphere grains. | Reproduction of published roller results gave **5.6%** mean relative error; a second blade benchmark gave about **10.8%**, falling below 2% at 50–100 mm/s. | Validation is mainly against prior simulations rather than an independent physical spreading experiment; dry-contact assumptions omit moisture and binder. (qabani2026discreteelementanalysis pages 7-9) |
| **EB-PBF rake DEM — Kelley and Ramulu (2024)** | Build-platform coverage, packing density and particle-shape effects at 50, 200 and 400 µm layers; irregular particles increased jamming and void formation. | Coverage and packing were compared qualitatively with experimental sintered-powder observations. | No numerical recoating error was reported; equal computational particle counts changed delivered mass when multisphere particles replaced spheres. (kelley2024investigationsofparticleprocesspart pages 15-17) |
| **Sequential binder-jet DEM → CFD — Sang et al. (2025)** | DEM supplies bed geometry and porosity; finite-volume VOF predicts droplet penetration, lateral spreading and saturation under capillarity and wetting. | Corresponding single-layer printing experiments supported the overall workflow. | **Sequential, not two-way CFD–DEM:** particles are fixed as CFD walls, so liquid forces, binder-induced rearrangement and fluid feedback to recoating are absent. (sang2026numericalinvestigationof pages 3-5) |
| **Geometry-downscaled DEM calibration — Sani et al. (2026)** | Rotating-drum break, rest and avalanche energies, free-surface behavior and segregation; true PSD was retained while drum radius was reduced **1:5** and Froude number preserved. | Scaling was checked at several drum sizes against 150 experimental avalanche events; raw energy time series were supplied as supplementary data. | Drum response is only a proxy for recoating; correspondence to thin-layer blade or roller spreading remains unproven. (sani2026efficientdemcalibration pages 8-10, sani2026efficientdemcalibration pages 2-4) |
| **Consolidation-calibrated DEM transferred to spreading — Katagiri et al. (2025)** | Bayesian optimization fitted SJKR cohesion and rolling resistance to void ratio; the fitted set produced collective motion and an overly narrow, excessively cohesive spread bed. | Consolidation experiment: measured void ratio **0.783**, simulated **0.776** for a near-optimal set. Transfer to spreading **failed**. | Bayesian optimization finds a point estimate, not a posterior. Normal-force-dominated consolidation did not identify shear and separation behavior needed for spreading. (katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 1-2, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 9-11, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 6-9, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 14-15) |

A published Bayesian-optimization study reproduced consolidation yet produced an excessively cohesive bed when its parameters were transferred to spreading. A practical *proposed* likelihood uses a continuous error model for mass and afterflow, a Bernoulli/binomial model for no-flow events, and a separate tap-response component. Treat cohesion–rolling-friction and wall-friction–packing trade-offs as identifiability questions. The observed **105 mg/rev** salt match without fitted parameters is an excellent forward check, but cannot identify the contact parameters of the other 12 powders. A published consolidation-only calibration provides a concrete warning about transfer to shear-dominated spreading. (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000043)
3. **Make posterior inference computationally feasible, and distinguish it from Bayesian optimization.** At **26–30 CPU-min per revolution**, 100 full-revolution evaluations cost approximately **43–50 CPU-hours**, before replication or multiple operating points. First screen parameters with a reduced, demonstrably representative outlet or experimental design; fit a multi-output emulator with predictive uncertainty, adaptively acquire additional DEM runs, and then sample a posterior that includes measurement noise and simulator discrepancy. Check the posterior against reserved tilt/speed/tap conditions and direct shear/density measurements. Bayesian *optimization* of a squared-error objective, as published for consolidation, finds candidate point estimates; it does not by itself deliver posterior uncertainty. Geometry-downscaled drum calibration may save cost, but particle enlargement or altered tool-gap/particle-size ratio must be independently tested before using it for the approximately 3 mm outlet or micron-scale recoater gap. (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000053, pqac-00000059)
4. **Test transfer in a separate spreading rig.** For gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047 first, measure blade and roller layers at several clearances and traverse speeds under controlled humidity. Register optical coverage and profilometric *Sa* with weighed areal loading and a trapped-volume/open-cup packing measurement; map PSD or composition along the travel direction for mixtures. Compare *posterior-predicted distributions* with held-out layers, not just a calibrated mean. Extend to irregular silicon grades and deliberately different sizes only after checking shape and cohesion-model adequacy. A doser fingerprint may be a useful prior or screening feature, but **its predictive value for recoating remains to be demonstrated**, especially because the doser’s tapping and wall contacts differ from blade/roller shear. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000037)

snippets: The powder spreading process can lead to powder layer defects such as porosity, poor surface roughness and particle segregation.

The model results show that interaction between particle and the powder spreading rake leads to noticeable variation in packing density, surface roughness, dynamic angle of repose (AOR), particle size distribution, and particle segregation.
The coarser particles (= 67 µm in average diameter) showed a larger dynamic AOR of 45° compared to the finer particles of 36° (= 23 µm in average diameter).

They showed that two different powders with similar apparent packing densities of 2.61 g/ml and 2.60 g/ml can lead to significant differences in porosity level, i.e. 20–30 pores per layer and 100 pores per layer.
Higher roller velocity and larger PSD lead to lower packing density and inferior powder bed surface roughness.
They reported that lower translational velocities achieved better powder bed quality, and that particles can be segregated during the spreading process.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides primary quantitative-simulation context for powder spreading in powder bed fusion, especially DEM studies using an idealised vertical blade and comparisons with roller spreading. Fouda and Bayly modeled spherical, mono-sized, non-cohesive Ti6Al4V particles and identified three causes of reduced deposited-layer packing fraction: shear-induced dilation when motion begins, dilation and rearrangement while particles pass through the blade gap, and particle inertia after deposition. Their results indicate that the mean normalized velocity in the shear layer is critical: higher values produce lower deposited packing fraction. Increasing gap thickness raises packing fraction, whereas increasing blade velocity lowers it. The excerpt also summarizes related DEM work showing that higher spreading speed increases surface roughness, broader particle-size distributions increase roughness, and increasing roller or blade velocity reduces layer quality as measured by surface roughness and packing density. A roller was reported to produce better layer quality than a blade for rod-shaped polymer particles. Powder-bed formation simulations further measured packing fraction and coordination number, both increasing with bed height and compression. The text states that deposited-layer uniformity and packing density influence final part porosity and bulk density. However, this excerpt does not provide DEM contact-law details, experimental validation, binder-jetting results, segregation metrics, open-source code, downloadable inputs, datasets, or comparisons with Hall/Carney, angle-of-repose, Hausner, shear-cell ffc, FT4, or rotating-drum avalanche tests.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative context relevant to powder-spreading simulations in LPBF, but it does not supply the requested primary quantitative evidence. It identifies cohesive energy density as a particularly influential DEM calibration parameter and states that simulations omitting cohesion overestimate powder mobility and fail to reproduce observed powder-bed characteristics. These measurements are therefore described as indicators rather than direct predictors of spreading performance, motivating process-specific testing and DEM simulations. The excerpt mentions packing density, powder-bed homogeneity, and repeatability as important outcomes, and notes that broad particle-size distributions can improve interstitial filling while excessive cohesion reduces mobility. contexts.context: The excerpt provides general guidance on relating powder-flow metrics to PBF spreading, but it does not report the requested direct experimental comparisons among Spierings (2015), Brocksieper (2026), Brika (2023), or related studies. It therefore contains no exact numerical results showing whether Hall flow, Hausner ratio, static angle of repose, shear-cell ffc, FT4 basic or specific energy, or rotating-drum avalanche metrics agree or disagree with measured layer density and roughness. The review emphasizes that flowability is an application-dependent umbrella term and that spreadability additionally involves layer homogeneity, packing/bulk density, and cohesion. It notes that particle size and size distribution often have the greatest effect on bulk flowability; spherical powders with few fines and a wide PSD can improve spreadability and layer density, although wide PSDs may also reduce flowability and increase segregation risk. The supplied text includes a proposed geometric guideline: layer thickness/D90 near 1.5 and D90/D10 near 5 for effective layering. It also gives generic flowability classifications: excellent powders have AoR 25–30°, CI ≤10%, HR 1.00–1.11, and ffc ≥10; very cohesive powders have AoR 56–65°, CI 32–37%, HR 1.46–1.59, and ffc ≤2. These are classification ranges, not correlations with measured layer roughness or density.

contexts.context: The excerpt from Brika and Brailovski (2023) does not report Hall flow, Hausner ratio, static angle of repose, shear-cell flowability (ffc), FT4 basic or specific energy, or rotating-drum avalanche measurements. Therefore, it cannot establish agreement or disagreement between those metrics and experimentally observed layer density or roughness, nor provide the requested cross-study numerical comparisons involving Spierings (2015), Brocksieper (2026), or direct experiments. It does provide relevant simulation-based powder-bed outcomes: the critical solid volume fraction for the elongated-particle assembly was identified as approximately 0.58, with the transition located between 0.575 and 0.585. Blade-head geometry strongly affected the resulting solid volume fraction, producing values from approximately 0.4 to approximately 0.58. Convex and concave blade profiles generated different particle-velocity fields; the concave profile exhibited an abrupt velocity change near the blade, interpreted as powder-grain clogging that degrades the bed. The study therefore links blade geometry and clogging behavior to simulated layer quality through solid volume fraction, but the excerpt contains no direct roughness values and no measurements from the named flowability instruments or tests.

The stated HR/CI classifications are: HR 1.00–1.11 and CI ≤10 indicate free-flowing to excellent flow; HR 1.12–1.18 and CI 11–15 indicate free-flowing to good flow; HR 1.19–1.25 and CI 16–20 indicate fair to passable flow; higher values indicate increasingly cohesive and poor flow. The flow-function metric ffc classifies powders as not flowing below 1, very cohesive from 1–2, cohesive from 2–4, easy-flowing from 4–10, and free-flowing above 10. However, ffc depends on consolidation stress, and conventional shear cells operate at stresses much higher than those in a powder heap before spreading. The Hall flowmeter is described as limited in sensitivity and problematic for cohesive powders. The excerpt qualitatively links low bulk density and poor packing with increased energy consumption, roughness, porosity, and unstable melt pools, but supplies no exact comparative dataset.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides qualitative guidance from Spierings et al. on comparing powder-flow metrics with powder-bed-based metal AM behavior, but it does not report the exact numerical results requested for Brocksieper 2026, Brika 2023, or related direct experiments. Spierings emphasizes that powder characterization should reproduce the manufacturing process as closely as possible, because AM involves small powder quantities, thin layers, dynamic movement, and potentially aerated powder. The paper states that its derived flowability value was correlated with an experience-based optical flowability evaluation, but the supplied pages do not give the correlation coefficients or layer-density/roughness data. Hausner ratio is described as widely used, with HR ≤ 1.25 associated with freely flowing powders and HR > 1.40 with cohesive/non-flowing powders; nevertheless, it did not correlate well with optical flowability and was judged unsuitable for AM because tapping and compression differ from recoating. Ring-shear testing is likewise considered poorly representative because it uses compressive loading. Hall flow/angle of repose is qualitatively related to flowability—lower angle and shorter discharge time indicate freer flow—but filling technique affects results, and the funnel opening can prevent some AM-suitable powders from flowing. No FT4 basic or specific energy, rotating-drum avalanche, static-angle numerical comparisons, or layer roughness/density values appear in the excerpt.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides Brocksieper et al. (2026) results for powder-layer arithmetic mean roughness (Sa), but it does not report the numerical results of Hall flow, Hausner ratio, static angle of repose, shear-cell flow function (ffc), FT4 basic or specific energy, rotating-drum avalanche measurements, or layer density. The study used 27 trials involving 316L, Alloy 718, and AlSi10Mg powders; blade, roller, and hopper recoaters; and recoater speeds of 50, 150, and 250 mm·s−1, with 15 layers per trial. Laser-scanner Sa data were used for further analysis because they generally produced slightly higher values and lower standard deviations than digital microscopy in 23 of 27 trials. ANOVA found that powder, recoater system, and recoater speed, including all two-factor and the three-factor interaction, significantly affected Sa; the regression model had R² = 90.64% and adjusted R² = 89.99%. Roller recoating produced the smoothest layers overall, while hopper recoating produced the greatest Sa; increasing speed generally increased Sa. AlSi10Mg had the highest average Sa and 316L the lowest, although significant interactions prevent isolated interpretation. The excerpt therefore supports comparisons with observed roughness only, not agreement or disagreement with the named flowability metrics or layer-density measurements.

contexts.context: An EOS M 290 validation used a shallow, centered 178-mm-wide, 5-mm-high “open cup” sampling area, built in 40-µm Alloy 718 layers. Weighing before/after powder removal produced minimum, measured, and maximum powder masses; packing density was calculated as \(PD=(m/\rho_s)/V_{sample}\). Five samples yielded mean \(PD_{min}=52.2\%\), \(PD_{measured}=52.4\%\), \(PD_{max}=52.4\%\), and \(PD_{nominal}=53.2\%\). DEM modeled ~260,000 particles over four layers, using measured PSD/density, friction 0.3/0.6, wall friction 0.4, stiffness 10 N/m, restitution 0.6, and compared multiple PD definitions.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. What physics-based simulations are used to predict powder spreadability and packing in powder-bed additive manufacturing (laser powder bed fusion, binder jetting, electron beam melting): DEM of blade and roller recoating with cohesive contact models, coarse-grained DEM, coupled DEM-CFD, and continuum models? Which spreadability metrics (packing fraction, surface roughness, coverage, mass per area, void fraction, segregation) are computed, how are they validated against spreading experiments, and how well do standard flowability tests (Hall flow, angle of repose, Hausner ratio, shear-cell ffc, FT4 energy, avalanche angle in a rotating drum) predict spreadability? Which open-source codes and published input decks exist?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a Revolution Powder Analyzer: a 100-mm-diameter, 35-mm-wide glass drum with imaging at 15 fps. After fluidisation (90 rpm, 30 s), flowability is measured at 0.6 rpm; three or more avalanches (up to 128) are recorded. Metrics include avalanche angle \(a_P\), surface-fractal dimension \(w_P\), and volume-expansion ratio \(\psi\), related to bulk/tap density and Hausner ratio. \(a_P\) and \(w_P\) generally follow log-normal distributions, though some powders are bimodal. A flowability limit of 2.5 is suggested for certain machines.

contexts.context: Haeri’s study uses particle-scale DEM of blade spreading, including realistic 3D reconstructed PEEK particles and collision stresses. Simple-shear simulations identify a jamming critical solid volume fraction of approximately **ϕcs = 0.58** (between **0.575–0.585**). Blade-profile optimization across **48 simulations** produced solid fractions from about **0.4 to 0.58**; geometry strongly affects bed quality. Convex profiles accelerate particles gradually, whereas concave profiles cause velocity discontinuities and powder clogging near the blade. The excerpt emphasizes volume fraction, jamming, particle velocities, and stress/flow-curve analysis, but reports no experimental validation or standard flowability correlations.

contexts.context: Haapa et al. validate a DEM powder-layering simulation against experimentally measured powder-bed density (PD) for Alloy 718 on an EOS M 290 using a 40 µm layer height. The experiment uses an open-cup sample positioned centrally near the dispenser. Powder mass is bounded by minimum, measured, and maximum estimates obtained from successive weighing and cleaning steps; sample volume is calculated from measured dimensions, and PD is computed from powder volume divided by sample volume. Across five samples, the experimental mean PD was 52.2% for PDmin (standard deviation 0.29%), 52.4% for PDmeasured (0.20%), and 52.4% for PDmax (0.22%). The nominal-CAD-volume estimate was higher and more variable: 53.2% mean with 0.56% standard deviation. The DEM model contains approximately 260,000 particles recoated in four 40 µm layers, uses the real recoater geometry and speed, and incorporates supplier PSD and density data plus calibrated/approximated contact parameters. Simulation density is evaluated using embedded-volume, powder-bed-extents, and intermediate definitions (PDmax-sim, PDmin-sim, and PDmeasured-sim), with both full-bed and central stable-area sampling. The excerpt does not provide the simulated PD numerical results or an explicit experiment–simulation agreement/error, so quantitative validation agreement cannot be calculated from these pages alone.

contexts.context: Lee et al. (2020) provide DEM validation against several experimental observables relevant to powder-bed quality. The strongest numerical agreement is for powder-bed height: the predicted height matches the measured value within a 1% error range. Dynamic angle of repose (AOR) is also compared over time; although the experiment shows an initial abrupt increase attributed potentially to atmospheric moisture and cohesive-bond effects, the model reproduces the subsequent variation reasonably well. Experimental and simulated powder-pile images are compared at multiple spreading positions. Both show progressive pile-volume reduction as the rake moves the powder, and both reproduce the plateau region at the pile top and its disappearance during spreading. For particle-size distribution (PSD), the initial simulated distribution corresponds to measurements, while measured and predicted PSDs are compared before and during deposition. The model predicts coarsening in the pile ahead of the rake during spreading and reports a finer PSD shift with increasing rake velocity in the recoating layer. The excerpt does not provide a direct numerical validation of captured mass or measured topography, and packing-density results appear primarily predictive rather than experimentally quantified. It reports approximately a 5% simulated density decrease when rake velocity is increased fivefold, alongside qualitative experimental surface-uniformity comparisons.

contexts.context: The excerpt validates DEM powder-bed packing using packing density (PD). Five open-cup samples had measured PD 52.2–52.6%, mean 52.4%, SD 0.20%; all PDmin/measured/max were 51–53%. Simulated PD depended strongly on sampling: in a stable region, PDmeasured-sim was 52% (matching experiment), while PDmin-sim and PDmax-sim were 45% and 58%. Using the full bed produced 49% measured-sim because thinner end regions added void space. Thus, validation requires matching sampling geometry and stable regions; measurement-method uncertainty exceeded experimental cleaning uncertainty.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. What physics-based simulations are used to predict powder spreadability and packing in powder-bed additive manufacturing (laser powder bed fusion, binder jetting, electron beam melting): DEM of blade and roller recoating with cohesive contact models, coarse-grained DEM, coupled DEM-CFD, and continuum models? Which spreadability metrics (packing fraction, surface roughness, coverage, mass per area, void fraction, segregation) are computed, how are they validated against spreading experiments, and how well do standard flowability tests (Hall flow, angle of repose, Hausner ratio, shear-cell ffc, FT4 energy, avalanche angle in a rotating drum) predict spreadability? Which open-source codes and published input decks exist?

contexts.context: The study evaluates AM powder flowability using optical flowability \(u_{\rm opt}\), Hausner ratio (HR), volume expansion ratio, avalanche angle \(a_P\), and surface fractal \(w_P\). HR poorly represented fine-metal-powder behavior: most had HR<1.25 (“freely flowing”) despite \(u_{\rm opt}>2.5\). Avalanche angles reached 70°, while others remained below 45°; both \(a_P\) and \(w_P\) correlated with optical flowability, reflecting interparticle forces, particle-size distribution, and shape. Distribution width also mattered: \(w_P\approx5.0\) marked deteriorating flow, with \(a_P\approx49^\circ\) (Fe) or \(54^\circ\) (Ni). A model predicted flowability with \(r^2=0.94\), RMSE=0.23.

contexts.context: The study measured powder-layer arithmetic roughness (Sa) using a digital microscope and laser scanner; the scanner’s larger area and lower variance better differentiated applications. ANOVA found significant powder × recoater system × speed interactions, so spreadability cannot be compared independently of equipment and speed. AlSi10Mg consistently spread worst, despite flow tests failing to predict this; only FT4 specific energy indicated its poor behavior. GranuDrum cohesive index (CI) tracked blade-recoater Sa trends versus speed, but absolute values and correlations varied by recoater; CI could extrapolate known powders, not predict unknown ones. Rotating-drum avalanche angle and dynamic angle showed no relationship.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. What physics-based simulations are used to predict powder spreadability and packing in powder-bed additive manufacturing (laser powder bed fusion, binder jetting, electron beam melting): DEM of blade and roller recoating with cohesive contact models, coarse-grained DEM, coupled DEM-CFD, and continuum models? Which spreadability metrics (packing fraction, surface roughness, coverage, mass per area, void fraction, segregation) are computed, how are they validated against spreading experiments, and how well do standard flowability tests (Hall flow, angle of repose, Hausner ratio, shear-cell ffc, FT4 energy, avalanche angle in a rotating drum) predict spreadability? Which open-source codes and published input decks exist?

contexts.context: Haeri (2017) uses device-scale DEM to optimize blade recoaters for PBF, where powder forms ~0.1-mm layers. Recoater geometry affects bed–spreader contact dynamics and void fraction; prior work found counter-rotating rollers produce lower void fractions than blades. A three-parameter super-elliptical blade profile was optimized using rod-shaped grains, achieving volume fractions near critical values. A new multi-sphere approximation represented realistic nonspherical grains; the optimized blade produced bed quality comparable to, or better than, a roller under realistic operating conditions. The paper also cites particle size, size distribution, morphology, angle of repose, flowability, volume fraction, and surface roughness as relevant factors.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides one powder-spreading simulation example: a conventional, particle-resolved DEM model of a vertical blade spreading an idealized heap of spherical, mono-sized, non-cohesive Ti6AlV4 particles across a horizontal substrate through a thin gap. The modeled physics include particle motion, shear-induced dilation when motion begins, dilation and rearrangement as particles pass through the gap, and particle inertia in the deposited layer. It evaluates process effects from gap thickness, blade velocity, and the velocity profile in the shear layer. The principal measured or computed validation quantities are deposited-layer packing fraction and its reduction relative to the initial heap; the article also frames layer uniformity and packing density as important manufacturing properties. The reported trends are that larger gap thickness increases packing fraction, while higher blade velocity and higher mean normalized shear-layer velocity reduce it. The study is mechanistic and potentially adaptable to other materials, particle morphologies, and surface properties, but the excerpt does not report experimental validation. Its limits are substantial for comparison with coarse-grained DEM, CFD-DEM, binder-liquid, continuum granular, or MPM approaches: it represents dry, non-cohesive, monodisperse spherical particles, uses an idealized blade geometry, and contains no gas-flow, liquid-binder, continuum, or coarse-graining treatment. Therefore, it supports a dry DEM benchmark rather than examples of the other requested model classes.

Haeri et al. (2017) used EDEM to simulate PEEK powder delivery with roller and blade spreaders. The modeled physics included particle shape, represented by elliptical particles assembled from multiple spheres, aspect ratio, spreader type, and operating conditions such as translational velocity. Powder-bed quality was evaluated using surface roughness and solid volume fraction (also described as volume fraction or solid volume), linking the simulations to measurable bed morphology and packing. The reported validation/comparison was primarily between simulated spreader configurations rather than against explicitly stated experiments. The roller produced better powder-bed quality than the blade, while larger particle aspect ratios and higher spreader translational velocities degraded quality. General DEM limitations noted in the excerpt include dependence on contact-model parameters and material properties, including friction, restitution, stiffness, particle size, density, and Poisson’s ratio. Using reduced Young’s modulus accelerates computation but can alter particle dynamics; reductions down to 0.001 of the actual modulus did not affect one mixing result, whereas further reduction decreased velocity gradients and mixing rate. No gas-flow, liquid-binder, continuum, MPM, coarse-graining, or quantitative experimental validation examples are supplied here.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes a coupled-style powder-bed and binder-liquid simulation, but not a powder-spreadability study using coarse-grained DEM, CFD–DEM gas flow, or continuum granular/MPM formulations. The powder is modeled with particle-resolved DEM in LIGGGHTS, using Newtonian translation and rotation, Hertz–Mindlin contact mechanics, Coulomb friction, simplified JKR cohesion, gravity, and an EPSD2 rolling-resistance torque. The liquid/gas problem is modeled separately with finite-volume Navier–Stokes equations in ANSYS Fluent using a transient VOF formulation, laminar incompressible Newtonian phases, volume-fraction-dependent density and viscosity, advection of liquid fraction, CSF surface tension, and contact-angle-based wall wetting. The numerical workflow and physics are therefore relevant to binder infiltration/migration through a powder bed rather than spreading dynamics or gas-driven powder transport. Reported checks include monitoring particle-size distribution and powder-bed density to maintain target effective pore throats, plus mesh-quality metrics (average skewness 0.03 and orthogonal quality 0.97). No direct experimental validation measurements, coarse-graining strategy, gas-flow spreading validation, continuum granular model, or MPM model are provided in this excerpt. Limitations include fixed particle positions as walls, idealized laminar/isothermal Newtonian phases, and the assumption that a 1.0 μm gap has negligible influence on migration.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides powder-spreadability examples based on conventional particle-scale DEM, rather than coarse-grained DEM, CFD–DEM gas-flow or binder-liquid coupling, or continuum granular/MPM models. The simulated physics include particle geometry and shape representation, viscoelastic contact forces, frictional boundaries, JKR-type surface adhesion, non-bonded van der Waals attraction, and variable inter-particle cohesion. Recoating simulations examine deposited-layer roughness and packing density as functions of blade translational velocity; the excerpt notes that elongated particle shape can preserve higher packing density at lower recoating velocities. Validation is primarily macroscopic and experimental: simulated bulk packing density is compared with measured values for fine silica-glass powders with particle sizes approximately 4–52 micrometers. Viscoelastic-only models agree for larger particles but fail for smaller ones; adding adhesion improves agreement, while the full viscoelastic-plus-adhesive-plus-van-der-Waals model reproduces the measured packing fraction across the complete size interval. For spreading layers, cohesion is assessed through packing structure, local density, surface roughness, and local structural anisotropy using the Qk measure and Bond number. Around Bo approximately 10, the layer transitions from homogeneous to heterogeneous and roughness increases; at Bo approximately 30, dense and loose regions coexist. The excerpt does not report gas-flow, liquid-binder, coarse-grained, continuum, or MPM simulations, nor their validation or limitations.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide specific powder-spreadability examples using coarse-grained DEM, CFD–DEM gas flow, binder-liquid coupling, continuum granular models, or MPM. It does, however, identify relevant modeling physics and validation principles. DEM can represent particle-scale kinematics, collisions, contact forces, cohesion, wall interactions, and—when augmented—bond formation, liquid bridges, breakage, or agglomeration. For processes involving changing particles, such as granulation or milling, ordinary rigid-particle DEM is insufficient because final size or product distributions require calibrated transformation laws. Suggested experimental anchors include particle-size and shape measurements, shear-cell or angle-of-repose data, compression/contact tests, flow-function measurements, wall-friction tests, and operational process measurements. For feeders and die filling, useful validation quantities include feed factor, mass-flow variability, residence time, tablet weight, and downstream quality measures, rather than flow visualization alone. The excerpt emphasizes that validation should cover relevant material properties and operating conditions. It also warns that transformation, breakage, and cohesive parameters may be material-, formulation-, equipment-, or mill-specific, limiting transferability. These points are applicable to spreadability simulations, but the requested model classes and gas-flow or binder-liquid case studies are absent from the supplied pages.

For coarse-grained DEM, simplifying particle shape, narrowing the size distribution, or representing particles as parcels improves computational feasibility, but can alter contact number, mass scaling, cohesion, segregation, and flow behaviour. contexts.context: The chapter uses DEM to simulate powder spreading with rakes and rollers, including realistic particle-size distributions, friction, adhesion, van der Waals forces, and non-spherical multisphere particles. JKR adhesion and van der Waals interactions are both essential for quantitative agreement with experiments. Simulations release ~6,500 particles and predict packing density and surface roughness as functions of recoating velocity and particle-size distribution. Local packing density alone misses structural defects; threshold-free local structural anisotropy better distinguishes homogeneous non-cohesive from heterogeneous cohesive layers. Thermal effects, particle shape, heat transfer, and vibrating recoaters are also highlighted.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. What physics-based simulations are used to predict powder spreadability and packing in powder-bed additive manufacturing (laser powder bed fusion, binder jetting, electron beam melting): DEM of blade and roller recoating with cohesive contact models, coarse-grained DEM, coupled DEM-CFD, and continuum models? Which spreadability metrics (packing fraction, surface roughness, coverage, mass per area, void fraction, segregation) are computed, how are they validated against spreading experiments, and how well do standard flowability tests (Hall flow, angle of repose, Hausner ratio, shear-cell ffc, FT4 energy, avalanche angle in a rotating drum) predict spreadability? Which open-source codes and published input decks exist?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes DEM solving six-degree-of-freedom Newtonian particle motion. Hertz–Mindlin contact uses Coulomb friction, \(F_t=\mu F_n\); SJKR adds cohesion \(F_{\rm Coh}=C_dA_{ij}n_{ij}\), with contact area defined by particle radii and separation. EPSD2 models rolling resistance, capped by \(T_r^{\max}=\mu_rR_{\rm eff}F_n\). Coupled CFD uses finite-volume Navier–Stokes equations and VOF for immiscible liquid–gas flow, including surface tension via \(F_\sigma=\sigma\kappa\nabla\alpha_l\), wall contact angle, and PISO coupling in ANSYS Fluent.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports DEM recoating validation using packing density (PD). Simulated stable-bed PD ranged 45–58%; the preferred sampling method gave 52%, matching experiment within one percentage point (repeat: 53%). Full-bed PD was up to three percentage points lower because powder was absent near recoater travel ends. Blade compression produced apparent 95% PD, particle overlap, and an unrealistic decompression wave, indicating spring-constant calibration needs. Recoating also caused fine-particle spray, size segregation/percolation, vortex-like flow, and incomplete, nonuniform first-layer coverage. Randomized particle generation caused minor repeat variability.

contexts.context: The 2025 ceramic binder-jetting study reports overall powder-bed packing densities of 0.6651 and 0.6517, with negligible transverse variation (Y1–Y3: 0.6516, 0.6521, 0.6512). DEM and experiments found bimodal 5/20 µm powder segregated during spreading: fines deposited first and coarse particles accumulated at the trailing edge. Packing density decreased along the spreading direction; fine-dominated regions packed densely, while coarse regions had larger voids. Binder droplets further ejected or rearranged particles, reducing green-part density. Smaller powders (1 and 5 µm) flowed better when heated; 10 and 20 µm powders flowed well at both temperatures.

contexts.context: A FLOW-3D recoating simulation tracked four layers (nominal depths 80, 120, 160, and 200 μm). It predicted incomplete, nonuniform first-layer coverage, particle-size segregation, blade-front compression/decompression, powder spray, and a low-depth dip at the travel end. Packing density (PD) was the principal metric. An “open cup” experiment validated PD: five trials averaged 52% with 0.2% standard deviation, though validation beds were ~20× thicker than simulations. Major uncertainties included coarse 10-class PSD, spherical particles, simplified friction, wall effects, omitted platform motion/vibration, and measurement-volume discrepancies.

We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. What physics-based simulations are used to predict powder spreadability and packing in powder-bed additive manufacturing (laser powder bed fusion, binder jetting, electron beam melting): DEM of blade and roller recoating with cohesive contact models, coarse-grained DEM, coupled DEM-CFD, and continuum models? Which spreadability metrics (packing fraction, surface roughness, coverage, mass per area, void fraction, segregation) are computed, how are they validated against spreading experiments, and how well do standard flowability tests (Hall flow, angle of repose, Hausner ratio, shear-cell ffc, FT4 energy, avalanche angle in a rotating drum) predict spreadability? Which open-source codes and published input decks exist?

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the Bayesian-optimization result as k = 48,779.3 J/m3 and mr = 0.60 (the article otherwise denotes the friction-related parameter as μr). The optimization used a surrogate model mapping (k, μr) to void ratio; a Random Forest surrogate was selected because it achieved the highest hold-out-validation R2, reducing evaluation time from about 8 hours for a DEM run to less than 1 second. A parametric study found that varying the EI exploration parameter wa from 0.01 to 1.0 produced the same optimum, indicating negligible influence under the tested conditions. Transfer to powder spreading failed: the consolidation-calibrated adhesion produced collective particle motion and an overly narrow powder bed, suggesting overestimated adhesion. Lowering k to 15,833 J/m3 generated a sparse powder-bed structure consistent with prior experiments, while reduced k generally broadened the bed. The provided pages do not state software licensing/repository details or public data availability, and they do not explain the conceptual distinction between Bayesian optimization and full Bayesian inference. They only describe Bayesian optimization as an iterative optimization workflow using an acquisition-function exploration parameter and surrogate predictions.

contexts.context: The excerpt states that Bayesian optimization was used sequentially to identify DEM parameters by minimizing the squared error between experimentally measured and DEM-predicted powder-bed void ratios during consolidation. The parameter cases discussed include cohesion-related k = 48,000 J/m3 with rotational-resistance parameter mr = 0.5 or 0, and a no-cohesion case; the excerpt also emphasizes matching the stress-to-Young’s-modulus ratio σ/E to preserve the leading nondimensional scaling. Validation was performed against consolidation void-ratio data across several applied stresses, including the experimental 9 kPa condition. The resulting consolidation-calibrated parameter set was then applied to powder spreading, but it did not accurately reproduce spreading, because consolidation is dominated by normal interparticle forces whereas spreading is dominated by contact separation, sliding, tangential forces, and shear. The authors therefore propose shear-specific observables such as bulk density, area coverage, and shear metrics, with possible reassessment of scaling and parameters. This excerpt does not provide software details, a public code repository, or data-availability information. It also does not explicitly distinguish Bayesian optimization from full Bayesian inference; it only describes Bayesian optimization as a sequential parameter-search/identification method minimizing squared error, rather than presenting posterior-distribution inference.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports a two-parameter Bayesian optimization for DEM consolidation: particle–particle stiffness k was searched over 10^2–10^5 J/m3 and rolling friction coefficient μr over 0.05–0.7. Five initial cases were used (four bound combinations plus the midpoint), followed by 100 iterations using a Gaussian-process model and expected-improvement acquisition. The best listed result was k = 47,500 J/m3 and μr = 0.5, with a void ratio of 0.776; the objective minimized the squared difference between experimental and DEM void ratios. The identified parameters were then used in a powder-spreading simulation, initially depositing 50,000 particles and moving a rectangular coater at 25 mm/s. This excerpt does not provide enough information to determine a separate validation protocol, whether transfer to spreading failed, or the outcome of that spreading simulation. It also does not state that data are publicly available or identify a public data repository. The software information given is GPyOpt 1.2.6, with GPy 1.13.2, NumPy 1.26.4, and Python 3.9. Conceptually, the described procedure is Bayesian optimization—sequentially selecting parameter evaluations through a surrogate and acquisition function—not full Bayesian inference over a posterior distribution of parameters; however, that distinction is not explicitly discussed in the excerpt. Noise handling was disabled in the reported table despite discussion of noisy experimental measurements.

Their calibration was validated against powder-consolidation experiments: the optimized pair reproduced the experimentally measured void ratio under confined loading. Consequently, the study argues that powder-bed AM calibration should include shear-sensitive experimental metrics and scaling considerations, rather than relying only on consolidation data. contexts.context: The excerpt states that Bayesian optimization was used to identify DEM parameters by minimizing the squared error between experimentally measured and simulated powder-bed void ratios during consolidation. The optimization proceeded sequentially; although the optimum was not reached within twelve trials, parameter sets close to it appeared by the fifth trial. Candidate selection incorporated user judgment in addition to Gaussian-process regression. The identified consolidation parameter set was dominated by inter-particle normal forces and reproduced consolidation behavior, but it did not transfer successfully to powder spreading or powder-bed formation. contexts.context: The excerpt reports DEM simulations comparing a roller with an optimized blade for powder-bed spreading. Using mixed particle Types 1–6 at three spreader velocities, the optimized blade produced bed volume fractions nearly matching the roller: it was 0.4% lower at 0.03 velocity but up to 2% higher at greater velocities, indicating less sensitivity and potentially higher productivity. Blade-generated beds also had lower surface roughness at every velocity. A new algorithm generated scalable multi-sphere approximations from STL powder shapes for realistic PBF particles. The work used open-source LIGGGHTS-style DEM and provides a public dataset (Haeri, 2016).
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. What physics-based simulations are used to predict powder spreadability and packing in powder-bed additive manufacturing (laser powder bed fusion, binder jetting, electron beam melting): DEM of blade and roller recoating with cohesive contact models, coarse-grained DEM, coupled DEM-CFD, and continuum models? Which spreadability metrics (packing fraction, surface roughness, coverage, mass per area, void fraction, segregation) are computed, how are they validated against spreading experiments, and how well do standard flowability tests (Hall flow, angle of repose, Hausner ratio, shear-cell ffc, FT4 energy, avalanche angle in a rotating drum) predict spreadability? Which open-source codes and published input decks exist?
