contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. What physics-based simulations are used to predict powder spreadability and packing in powder-bed additive manufacturing (laser powder bed fusion, binder jetting, electron beam melting): DEM of blade and roller recoating with cohesive contact models, coarse-grained DEM, coupled DEM-CFD, and continuum models? Which spreadability metrics (packing fraction, surface roughness, coverage, mass per area, void fraction, segregation) are computed, how are they validated against spreading experiments, and how well do standard flowability tests (Hall flow, angle of repose, Hausner ratio, shear-cell ffc, FT4 energy, avalanche angle in a rotating drum) predict spreadability? Which open-source codes and published input decks exist?

contexts.context: The excerpt provides relevant evidence concerning DEM–CFD modelling, computational savings through particle coarse-graining, and sensitivity to particle upscaling. The study uses FELMI, described as an in-house DEM–CFD solver, coupled with a signed-distance-function immersed-boundary method for moving and arbitrarily shaped walls, coarse-grained DEM for reducing particle numbers, and a rotational-resistance model for representing nonspherical particle effects with spherical computational particles. The coarse-grained approach represents multiple original particles by one computational particle while maintaining energy consistency and substantially reducing computational cost. Validation in a linear shoe–die filling system found excellent agreement between original-particle and coarse-grained simulations. However, simply enlarging particles by three times their original diameter produced markedly different macroscopic filling behaviour, specifically faster filling attributed to reduced air-drag effects. This directly supports the need for sensitivity checks when scaling particle geometry or using computationally enlarged particles. The excerpt does not identify MercuryDPM, LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS, CFDEM, OpenFOAM, EDEM, Fluent, FLOW-3D, or the Haeri dataset/DOI, and therefore supplies no evidence about those software packages, open-source versus commercial licensing, publicly accessible inputs, or dataset availability.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides evidence relevant to cost-saving geometry simplification and sensitivity to particle upscaling, but it does not identify specific DEM software packages, datasets, or coupling frameworks. It states that industrial-scale modelling commonly requires simplified particle shapes, narrowed size distributions, or coarse-grained parcels because representing every physical particle is often impractical. Spherical particles reduce computational expense, whereas clumps and other non-spherical representations improve representation of interlocking and rotational resistance at greater computational cost. The review cautions that coarse graining is not dynamically neutral: it can alter contact number, mass scaling, cohesion, and segregation behaviour. Therefore, an upscaled model must be recalibrated and independently validated rather than assumed equivalent to the original powder. The excerpt also notes that explicit DEM becomes expensive for finer or stiffer particles because the time step must remain small relative to contact dynamics. Calibration should use bulk tests and reflect the intended process regime; multi-objective calibration is preferable where possible. No evidence is supplied here for MercuryDPM, LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS, a Haeri dataset DOI, CFDEM/OpenFOAM, or comparisons with commercial EDEM, Fluent, or FLOW-3D.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides relevant evidence about cost-saving particle upscaling in DEM–CFD simulations, but it does not identify specific DEM software packages such as MercuryDPM, LIGGGHTS, or LAMMPS, nor does it mention the Haeri dataset, a DOI, publicly accessible input files, or open-source coupling frameworks such as CFDEM or OpenFOAM. It also contains no comparison with commercial software such as EDEM, Fluent, or FLOW-3D. The strongest relevant finding concerns the distinction between coarse-graining and simple geometric enlargement. Coarse-grained particles, used with rotational resistance, reproduced the macroscopic filling behaviour of the original particles while substantially reducing computational cost. By contrast, simply enlarging particles to three times the original diameter produced markedly different and faster filling because of reduced air-drag effects. This indicates that particle upscaling is sensitive to how scaling is implemented and that preserving relevant particle physics—especially non-sphericity and rotational resistance—is important. The study describes a coupled DEM–CFD framework for industrial powder die filling involving moving complex boundaries and large particle numbers. A separate study uses DEM to model a drag-force-flow sensor and assess how particle size, density, and friction affect measured probe forces, with machine-learning models intended to predict particle properties. These studies support general DEM/CFD methodological relevance, but not the requested software, dataset-accessibility, or open-source-versus-commercial comparisons.

contexts.context: A 2025 study identifies DEM parameters using Bayesian optimization because exhaustive simulations are expensive. It minimizes squared error between FT4 consolidation void ratio and DEM void ratio after 9 kPa compression, calibrating JKR surface energy \(k\) and rolling friction \(\mu_r\). LIGGGHTS-PUBLIC 3.8.0 uses Hertz–Mindlin contacts, SJKR cohesion, and constant-directional-torque rolling resistance. The HX powder is near-spherical, 10–40 µm (mean 29 µm), and 500,000 particles are simulated. Identified parameters are transferred to powder-spreading simulations and compared with prior studies to validate parameter transferability.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. What physics-based simulations are used to predict powder spreadability and packing in powder-bed additive manufacturing (laser powder bed fusion, binder jetting, electron beam melting): DEM of blade and roller recoating with cohesive contact models, coarse-grained DEM, coupled DEM-CFD, and continuum models? Which spreadability metrics (packing fraction, surface roughness, coverage, mass per area, void fraction, segregation) are computed, how are they validated against spreading experiments, and how well do standard flowability tests (Hall flow, angle of repose, Hausner ratio, shear-cell ffc, FT4 energy, avalanche angle in a rotating drum) predict spreadability? Which open-source codes and published input decks exist?

contexts.context: The study uses DEM with Hertz–Mindlin (no-slip) contacts for dry particles, Coulomb friction, damping, and reduced roller stiffness/density to permit larger time steps while treating the roller as rigid. For binder-jetting, powder-bed density (PBD) is computed per grid as particle mass divided by material density and grid volume; average PBD and spatial variation/segregation via standard deviation or FSD are reported. Validation against Zhang et al.’s Al₂O₃ simulations yielded 5.6% mean relative error. PA6 blade-speed validation reproduced decreasing packing density with speed, with ~10.8% mean error and <2% error at 50–100 mm/s.

contexts.context: The excerpt models electron-beam powder-bed spreading using LIGGGHTS, generating spherical, faceted (FDDE), and irregular undercut (SSAM) particles; irregular particles are approximated with multisphere CLUMP representations. Simulated raking shows that 50 μm layers have the poorest coverage, with distinct particle-free regions and poor packing, while 200–400 μm layers improve coverage and packing. Spherical particles pack better than SSAM particles at 400 μm, although increased layer height can promote jamming and void formation. Reported packing densities are comparable to experimentally measured sintered “moons.” Particle shape metrics include sphericity, aspect ratio, solidity, and circularity.

contexts.context: Haeri (2017) uses LAMMPS DEM to simulate blade powder spreading. Non-spherical rods are represented by rigid multi-sphere particles (2–4 spheroids), with aspect ratios \(A_r=1.5, 2.0, 2.5\), reducing computational cost. Particles are prepared by rainfall, with periodic boundaries laterally and rigid walls vertically; bottom-wall rolling friction uses \(l_r=0.005\). Contacts use a linear Hookean spring-dashpot model (\(e=0.5\), \(Y=3.7\) GPa, \(\nu=0.4\), \(j_n=1500\) N/m), selected for “low computational costs.” Blade designs are compared by volume fraction.

contexts.context: The study calibrates real-size-distribution DEM for AM powders using a rotating-drum avalanche experiment. Inconel 718 and Ti-6Al-4V have D10/D50/D90 of 51.73/78.32/113.9 and 50.1/69.8/97.1 µm. A fivefold drum-radius reduction (25 to 5 mm) preserves dynamics by matching Froude number, \(Fr=\omega^2R/g\), increasing angular velocity by \(\sqrt5\). DOE, surrogate modeling, and optimization fit break, rest, and avalanche specific-energy curves from 150 avalanches. RPA additionally measures surface topography, dynamic repose angle, and packing; avalanche angle is excluded because it depends strongly on drum radius.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. What physics-based simulations are used to predict powder spreadability and packing in powder-bed additive manufacturing (laser powder bed fusion, binder jetting, electron beam melting): DEM of blade and roller recoating with cohesive contact models, coarse-grained DEM, coupled DEM-CFD, and continuum models? Which spreadability metrics (packing fraction, surface roughness, coverage, mass per area, void fraction, segregation) are computed, how are they validated against spreading experiments, and how well do standard flowability tests (Hall flow, angle of repose, Hausner ratio, shear-cell ffc, FT4 energy, avalanche angle in a rotating drum) predict spreadability? Which open-source codes and published input decks exist?

# Physics-based prediction of powder-bed spreadability

**Bottom line.** Particle-resolved discrete-element modelling (DEM) is the best-supported way to predict *how a specified powder, recoater and operating condition* produce a bed. It can resolve coverage gaps, local packing, roughness and size segregation that a bulk-flow number cannot. Its predictions still require independent spreading measurements: fitting a powder to a doser, shear cell or consolidation test does not establish that its contact parameters transfer to a thin, rapidly sheared layer. A published Bayesian-optimization study reproduced consolidation yet produced an excessively cohesive bed when its parameters were transferred to spreading. (fouda2019ademstudy pages 1-2, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 1-2, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 14-15)

## Models, outputs and validation

In **blade or rake DEM**, particles move through a prescribed clearance under gravity, particle–particle and particle–wall forces. In **roller DEM**, traverse speed, rotation, roller diameter and gap additionally control compaction, jamming and shear. Common choices are Hertz–Mindlin normal/tangential contact, Coulomb sliding, a rolling-resistance torque and an adhesive law; published spreading models use either JKR adhesion or simplified JKR (SJKR). These are *different parameterizations*: an SJKR cohesion-energy-density value should not be interpreted as a JKR surface energy or an intrinsic material constant. Spheres efficiently represent near-spherical atomized alloys; bonded multisphere clumps better represent irregular or satellite-bearing particles at greater cost. Fouda and Bayly’s idealized blade study isolates shear dilation before and within the gap and inertial dilation after deposition: increasing blade speed decreased packing, whereas increasing the gap raised it. Roller studies likewise found layer thickness and traverse speed consequential, but their conclusions depend on the powder and recoater geometry. (fouda2019ademstudy pages 1-2, zhang2020discreteelementsimulation pages 3-5, angelidakis2025demsimulationof pages 1-4, brika2023anovelapparatus pages 3-5)

For comparison across simulations, define **local packing fraction** as solid particle volume divided by a *specified sampling volume*, **void fraction** as one minus that fraction, and **areal loading** as deposited mass divided by sampled area. Also report deposited height and its distribution, substrate **coverage** or uncovered-area fraction from registered images, surface-height roughness such as *Sa*, and species-resolved particle-size/composition maps along and across spreading. These observables are not interchangeable: a smooth surface does not establish a dense interior. Include the sampling depth, treatment of particles crossing its boundary, edge exclusions and number of layers with every reported packing value. Lee et al. assessed height, packing, roughness and size redistribution; binder-jet experiments demonstrate why directional segregation and local density must also be measured. (lee2020effectofparticle pages 1-2, lee2020effectofparticle pages 9-11, brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 9-10, shahed2025powderspreadingbehavior pages 10-11)

The following comparison separates direct experimental agreement from simulation-to-simulation benchmarking and unvalidated model possibilities. (lee2020effectofparticle pages 9-11, haapa2023validationofpowder pages 7-9, qabani2026discreteelementanalysis pages 7-9)

| Model/process and study | Predicted or observed layer metrics | Validation | Essential limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LPBF, particle-resolved blade DEM — Haapa et al. (2023)** | Packing density, layer thickness, coverage and PSD segregation. Central stable-region density was **52%**; changing the sampling-volume definition changed it from **45% to 58%**. | Open-cup Alloy 718 experiment measured **52.4% ± 0.20 percentage points**, agreeing with the analogous 52% simulation result. | Apparent accuracy is strongly ROI-dependent; only four layers and spherical particles were modeled, and randomized initialization shifted the analogous density from 52% to 53%. (haapa2023validationofpowder pages 7-9, haapa2023simulationofmetalb pages 84-89, haapa2023validationofpowder media 7454531e) |
| **LPBF, multilayer rake DEM — Lee et al. (2020)** | Bed height, packing density, roughness, dynamic angle of repose, PSD and segregation; fivefold higher rake speed reduced simulated density by about **5%**. | Predicted bed height was within **1%** of experiment; pile evolution and later dynamic-angle variation agreed qualitatively. | Initial dynamic-angle discrepancy was attributed to unmodeled moisture/cohesive effects; packing-density validation was not comparably quantified. (lee2020effectofparticle pages 9-11) |
| **Blade versus roller DEM — Haeri (2017)** | Solid volume fraction and surface roughness for nonspherical particles; optimized blade reached roller-like packing and up to **2% higher** volume fraction at higher tested speeds. | Primarily comparative simulation; realistic multisphere shapes were used, with an associated public simulation dataset. | Results depend on simplified contact mechanics and shape representation; a complete runnable input deck was not verified. (brika2023anovelapparatus pages 11-12, brika2023anovelapparatus pages 3-5) |
| **Roller DEM — Zhang et al. (2020)** | Powder-bed density versus traverse speed, roller rotation, diameter and layer thickness; larger thickness and diameter improved density, while higher traverse speed degraded it. | Friction was measured by ASTM D6773; surface energy was calibrated to repose/avalanche behavior. A later reproduction reported **5.6% mean relative error** against Zhang’s density results. | This is cross-study reproduction rather than direct machine-scale validation; Young’s modulus was reduced by two orders of magnitude. (zhang2020discreteelementsimulation pages 3-5, qabani2026discreteelementanalysis pages 7-9) |
| **Binder jetting, roller DEM plus experiment — Shahed et al. (2025)** | Directional size segregation and packing: 5 µm particles accumulated near the start and 20 µm particles toward the trailing edge; packing density dropped **7.65%** along the spreading direction. | Simulation and experiment agreed on the **direction** of segregation and density gradient; no numerical DEM–experiment error was reported. | Directional agreement is not a quantitatively validated packing prediction; binder impact subsequently rearranged or ejected particles. (shahed2025powderspreadingbehavior pages 10-11) |
| **Binder jetting, irregular raw-sediment roller DEM — Al Qabani et al. (2026)** | Local and mean packing density, density variability and segregation using reconstructed multisphere grains. | Reproduction of published roller results gave **5.6%** mean relative error; a second blade benchmark gave about **10.8%**, falling below 2% at 50–100 mm/s. | Validation is mainly against prior simulations rather than an independent physical spreading experiment; dry-contact assumptions omit moisture and binder. (qabani2026discreteelementanalysis pages 7-9) |
| **EB-PBF rake DEM — Kelley and Ramulu (2024)** | Build-platform coverage, packing density and particle-shape effects at 50, 200 and 400 µm layers; irregular particles increased jamming and void formation. | Coverage and packing were compared qualitatively with experimental sintered-powder observations. | No numerical recoating error was reported; equal computational particle counts changed delivered mass when multisphere particles replaced spheres. (kelley2024investigationsofparticleprocesspart pages 15-17) |
| **Sequential binder-jet DEM → CFD — Sang et al. (2025)** | DEM supplies bed geometry and porosity; finite-volume VOF predicts droplet penetration, lateral spreading and saturation under capillarity and wetting. | Corresponding single-layer printing experiments supported the overall workflow. | **Sequential, not two-way CFD–DEM:** particles are fixed as CFD walls, so liquid forces, binder-induced rearrangement and fluid feedback to recoating are absent. (sang2026numericalinvestigationof pages 3-5) |
| **Geometry-downscaled DEM calibration — Sani et al. (2026)** | Rotating-drum break, rest and avalanche energies, free-surface behavior and segregation; true PSD was retained while drum radius was reduced **1:5** and Froude number preserved. | Scaling was checked at several drum sizes against 150 experimental avalanche events; raw energy time series were supplied as supplementary data. | Drum response is only a proxy for recoating; correspondence to thin-layer blade or roller spreading remains unproven. (sani2026efficientdemcalibration pages 8-10, sani2026efficientdemcalibration pages 2-4) |
| **Consolidation-calibrated DEM transferred to spreading — Katagiri et al. (2025)** | Bayesian optimization fitted SJKR cohesion and rolling resistance to void ratio; the fitted set produced collective motion and an overly narrow, excessively cohesive spread bed. | Consolidation experiment: measured void ratio **0.783**, simulated **0.776** for a near-optimal set. Transfer to spreading **failed**. | Bayesian optimization finds a point estimate, not a posterior. Normal-force-dominated consolidation did not identify shear and separation behavior needed for spreading. (katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 1-2, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 9-11, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 6-9, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 14-15) |
| **Coarse-grained DEM/CFD status** | Can reduce particle count by representing many physical grains with one computational particle while rescaling interactions. | A non-AM shoe-filling example reproduced original-particle behavior; simply tripling particle diameter instead produced faster filling because air drag changed. | No retrieved AM recoating case provided independent, quantified validation of coarse-grained predictions for packing, roughness, coverage and segregation simultaneously. (goh2026bookofabstracts pages 31-33, goh2026bookofabstracts pages 33-36) |
| **Continuum granular/MPM recoating status** | In principle predicts bulk velocity, stress, free-surface evolution and solids fraction using constitutive laws rather than resolved contacts. | **No quantitatively validated continuum powder-spreading case was identified in the retrieved literature.** | Thin layers only a few particles deep, cohesion, jamming, discrete coverage holes and size segregation challenge continuum closure; DEM remains the dominant spreading model in this evidence set. (fouda2019ademstudy pages 1-2, angelidakis2025demsimulationof pages 8-11, qureshi2023developmentofa pages 238-243) |


*Table: Comparison of physics-based recoating models, their layer-quality outputs, validation evidence, and principal limitations. It distinguishes quantitative experimental validation from qualitative agreement, cross-simulation benchmarks, and unvalidated model classes.*

**The strongest numerical validation found illustrates a measurement hazard.** In an Alloy 718 LPBF open-cup experiment, five samples gave **52.4% mean packing fraction**, with **0.20 percentage-point standard deviation**. A four-layer DEM result was **52%** using a corresponding central sampling region. Merely changing the simulated sampling-volume definition yielded **45%, 52% or 58%**; sampling the entire bed rather than its stable central region also changed the answer. Thus, agreement to within a percentage point is meaningful only when experimental and simulated volumes are constructed alike. The cropped density-window comparison makes this dependence visible. Lee et al. independently reported recoated-bed height within **1%** of experiment, alongside qualitative agreement in pile motion, rather than a comparably precise experimental confirmation of every simulated packing or segregation output. (haapa2023validationofpowder pages 5-7, lee2020effectofparticle pages 9-11, haapa2023validationofpowder pages 7-9, haapa2023validationofpowder media 7454531e)

**Across processes.** Binder-jetting DEM uses the same dry recoating mechanics but particularly needs spatial packing and composition because these determine binder access and green-part heterogeneity. In a 5/20 µm alumina mixture, simulated and observed segregation both placed more fines early in the spreading direction and coarser particles later; the measured bed-packing decline along that direction was **7.65%**, but a point-by-point numerical DEM error was not established. For electron-beam powder-bed fusion, a study of reused feedstock simulated rake coverage and packing for spherical and irregular multisphere particles; it found poorly covered thin layers and shape-dependent jamming. Its recoating agreement was not reported as a numerical error. EBM also warrants process-specific temperature and powder-state validation rather than assuming ambient LPBF parameters transfer. (shahed2025powderspreadingbehavior pages 10-11, kelley2024investigationsofparticleprocesspart pages 15-17)

**Coupling and acceleration have narrower evidence.** A metal binder-jet study first made a 17-4PH bed with LIGGGHTS DEM, then passed fixed particle geometry to a finite-volume, volume-of-fluid simulation of liquid-binder wetting and penetration, checking the workflow against single-layer printing experiments. This is *sequential DEM → CFD*, not a demonstrated two-way gas–particle CFD–DEM predictor of recoating. Two-way CFD–DEM is appropriate when carrier-gas drag or gas-driven entrainment matters; liquid infiltration requires wetting and capillarity, not merely a gas-drag correction. Neither should be added to an ambient dry-recoating model without an experimentally motivated fluid effect. (sang2026numericalinvestigationof pages 3-5)

Coarse-grained DEM reduces particle count but changes the ratios among gravity, cohesion, contact forces and fluid drag unless its scaling rules preserve them. An industrial **shoe-filling**, *not AM recoating*, DEM–CFD example retained macroscopic behavior with a calibrated coarse-grained model, whereas simply tripling particle diameter made filling faster because air drag changed. Geometry reduction without enlarging particles is a different compromise: Sani et al. retained the real alloy size distribution in a rotating-drum calibration, reduced drum radius fivefold and adjusted speed to preserve Froude number. They explicitly did **not** establish that a drum-calibrated response predicts recoating. Continuum granular-flow, finite-volume or material-point formulations can represent averaged stresses, solids fraction and a moving free surface at larger scale; in the retrieved studies, however, there was **no independently quantified validation of a continuum recoater model** for fine-layer coverage gaps, roughness and segregation. These approaches are candidates for larger, well-resolved regions or hybrids, not a demonstrated replacement for particle-resolved thin-layer DEM. (goh2026bookofabstracts pages 31-33, sani2026efficientdemcalibration pages 2-4, fouda2019ademstudy pages 1-2, qureshi2023developmentofa pages 238-243)

## Do conventional flow tests predict spreadability?

**Not reliably as universal rankings.** Hall/Carney discharge interrogates an orifice and can return *no flow* for powder that a recoater can spread; angle of repose depends on its formation protocol; Hausner ratio reflects tapping rather than the weak confinement and shearing of recoating. Shear-cell flow function, *ffc*, depends on consolidation stress and usefully constrains yield behavior, but a value measured under substantial consolidation is not itself a prediction of a thin layer. FT4 blade energy and rotating-drum avalanching probe more dynamic states, yet their ability to rank powders remains conditional on test protocol, material and spreader. Use B213/B964, B212/B527, D7891/D6773, repose, sieving/laser diffraction and loss on drying as **independent characterization**, not interchangeable measures of spreading quality. For D6773 or FT4 shear, retain the full stress-dependent yield locus and wall-friction information where possible rather than reducing everything to one *ffc*. (spierings2016powderflowabilitycharacterisation pages 3-4, talebi2021characterisationofspreadability pages 28-33, brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 9-10, zhang2020discreteelementsimulation pages 3-5)

Two experiments show the distinction particularly clearly. Spierings et al. found that the Hausner ratio failed to track their **optical powder-flowability classification**, whereas a fitted combination of drum avalanche/surface descriptors achieved **R² = 0.94** against *that optical rating*. This is **not** an R² for measured recoated-layer packing or roughness. In a later **27-condition, 405-layer** comparison of 316L, Alloy 718 and AlSi10Mg across blade, roller and hopper recoaters at 50, 150 and 250 mm/s, Brocksieper et al. found significant powder × recoater × speed interactions in measured layer *Sa*. Alloy 718 did **not flow in the Hall funnel** yet could make blade/roller layers as smooth as, or smoother than, the more freely flowing 316L; AlSi10Mg gave the roughest layers, a ranking most conventional flow results did not anticipate. FT4 **specific energy** indicated its poorer behavior. Drum avalanche and dynamic angles did **not** correlate with observed application behavior in that study, although speed-dependent drum cohesive-index trends resembled **blade** roughness trends for powders already characterized. The authors explicitly did **not** establish prediction for an unknown powder or for roller/hopper systems. They measured surface roughness, **not bed density**. (spierings2016powderflowabilitycharacterisation pages 8-10, brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 7-9, brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 9-10, brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 4-5)

Accordingly, evaluate each conventional test against an actual, held-out spreading endpoint—coverage, *Sa*, areal mass or packing—**separately for each recoater and speed regime**. A significant within-alloy or within-machine association is useful screening evidence, not a transferable material law. (brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 9-10, spierings2016powderflowabilitycharacterisation pages 3-4)

## Open implementations and reproducibility

- **LIGGGHTS-PUBLIC 3.8.0** is directly relevant to the existing doser: Katagiri et al. publish a model specification using Hertz–Mindlin, `sjkr2` cohesion and `cdt` rolling resistance; Sang et al. use open-source LIGGGHTS for binder-jet bed generation. The published parameter table and equations are useful *starting descriptions*, **not a verified downloadable runnable recoater input deck** or transferable parameters. In particular, changing from constant-directional-torque rolling resistance to another rolling law requires recalibration. (katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 2-4, sang2026numericalinvestigationof pages 3-5, qureshi2023developmentofa pages 238-243)
- **LAMMPS** was used for Haeri’s blade-profile and multisphere recoating simulations; **MercuryDPM** and **YADE** are documented open granular-simulation packages that can serve as alternative modelling bases. The evidence retrieved does not establish a specific maintained, ready-to-run AM recoating example for each. **EDEM, ANSYS Fluent and FLOW-3D** appear in relevant studies but should not be represented as open-source substitutes. Check the version, license and implemented adhesion/rolling-law definitions before porting any deck. (brika2023anovelapparatus pages 3-5, qureshi2023developmentofa pages 238-243, sang2026numericalinvestigationof pages 3-5, haapa2023simulationofmetalb pages 89-94)
- A **published simulation dataset** is explicitly cited as Haeri, *Dataset—discrete element simulation of powder spreading in additive manufacturing* (2016), **DOI: 10.15129/c5993a8f-812d-46cf-bef5-92e985d12446**. The retrieved publication does **not** establish that this deposit includes the complete geometry, scripts, executable input deck and contact-law implementation needed for one-command reproduction. Haeri’s 2017 paper publishes geometry and contact-model details, and Sani et al. report supplementary experimental drum-energy series; neither fact alone verifies a runnable recoating deck. No fully verified downloadable open-source *recoating input deck* was located in the reviewed sources. (brika2023anovelapparatus pages 11-12, sani2026efficientdemcalibration pages 2-4)

## Recommended doser-to-spreader calibration experiment

1. **Separate measured particle properties from inferred effective contacts.** For each powder, measure particle skeletal density, number/volume size distributions, morphology, water content and controlled relative humidity; record PLA/PETG surface condition and powder history. Set DEM size and density from these measurements. Infer *effective model-specific* particle–particle and particle–wall adhesion, sliding and rolling parameters, rather than claiming that a uniquely inferred `sjkr2` coefficient is intrinsic cohesion. The need to account for shape, adhesion and particle-size distribution in packing has experimental DEM support. (angelidakis2025demsimulationof pages 8-11, angelidakis2025demsimulationof pages 1-4, zhang2020discreteelementsimulation pages 3-5)
2. **Calibrate against several distinct features, not salt throughput alone.** Use replicated mass/revolution versus tilt and rpm, per-tap released mass, stop-afterflow curves and zero-flow increments with their uncertainty; include fill level, initialization and wall/material state as inputs. A practical *proposed* likelihood uses a continuous error model for mass and afterflow, a Bernoulli/binomial model for no-flow events, and a separate tap-response component. Treat cohesion–rolling-friction and wall-friction–packing trade-offs as identifiability questions. The observed **105 mg/rev** salt match without fitted parameters is an excellent forward check, but cannot identify the contact parameters of the other 12 powders. A published consolidation-only calibration provides a concrete warning about transfer to shear-dominated spreading. (katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 1-2, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 11-14, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 14-15)
3. **Make posterior inference computationally feasible, and distinguish it from Bayesian optimization.** At **26–30 CPU-min per revolution**, 100 full-revolution evaluations cost approximately **43–50 CPU-hours**, before replication or multiple operating points. First screen parameters with a reduced, demonstrably representative outlet or experimental design; fit a multi-output emulator with predictive uncertainty, adaptively acquire additional DEM runs, and then sample a posterior that includes measurement noise and simulator discrepancy. Check the posterior against reserved tilt/speed/tap conditions and direct shear/density measurements. Bayesian *optimization* of a squared-error objective, as published for consolidation, finds candidate point estimates; it does not by itself deliver posterior uncertainty. Geometry-downscaled drum calibration may save cost, but particle enlargement or altered tool-gap/particle-size ratio must be independently tested before using it for the approximately 3 mm outlet or micron-scale recoater gap. (katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 4-6, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 2-4, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 14-15, sani2026efficientdemcalibration pages 8-10, sani2026efficientdemcalibration pages 2-4)
4. **Test transfer in a separate spreading rig.** For gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047 first, measure blade and roller layers at several clearances and traverse speeds under controlled humidity. Register optical coverage and profilometric *Sa* with weighed areal loading and a trapped-volume/open-cup packing measurement; map PSD or composition along the travel direction for mixtures. Compare *posterior-predicted distributions* with held-out layers, not just a calibrated mean. Extend to irregular silicon grades and deliberately different sizes only after checking shape and cohesion-model adequacy. A doser fingerprint may be a useful prior or screening feature, but **its predictive value for recoating remains to be demonstrated**, especially because the doser’s tapping and wall contacts differ from blade/roller shear. (haapa2023validationofpowder pages 7-9, shahed2025powderspreadingbehavior pages 10-11, brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 9-10, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 1-2)

| **Continuum granular/MPM recoating status** | In principle predicts bulk velocity, stress, free-surface evolution and solids fraction using constitutive laws rather than resolved contacts. | **No quantitatively validated continuum powder-spreading case was identified in the retrieved literature.** | Thin layers only a few particles deep, cohesion, jamming, discrete coverage holes and size segregation challenge continuum closure; DEM remains the dominant spreading model in this evidence set. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029) |


*Table: Comparison of physics-based recoating models, their layer-quality outputs, validation evidence, and principal limitations. It distinguishes quantitative experimental validation from qualitative agreement, cross-simulation benchmarks, and unvalidated model classes.*

info.query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. What physics-based simulations are used to predict powder spreadability and packing in powder-bed additive manufacturing (laser powder bed fusion, binder jetting, electron beam melting): DEM of blade and roller recoating with cohesive contact models, coarse-grained DEM, coupled DEM-CFD, and continuum models? Which spreadability metrics (packing fraction, surface roughness, coverage, mass per area, void fraction, segregation) are computed, how are they validated against spreading experiments, and how well do standard flowability tests (Hall flow, angle of repose, Hausner ratio, shear-cell ffc, FT4 energy, avalanche angle in a rotating drum) predict spreadability? Which open-source codes and published input decks exist?
